Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw the attention of the House to a certain matter, and for that purpose I would move the adjournment of the House. In the county of Glengarry we have several societies, principally Scottish and French. These societies at different times hold celebrations, which we consider a right and proper thing to do, and on these occasions we frequently have men of eminence to take part. Last Wednesday the Earl of Dundonald consented to meet the Scottish clans of Glengarry at their celebration. The arrangements were all completed the night before, and on Wednesday morning he was awaited by a number of the Scottish people who had gathered at the railway station. On my arrival on the same train by which he was expected to come, it was found that Lord Dundonald was not present. On inquiring of the cause by putting the telegraph wires in motion, we found that he had received that morning a written message coming from the Bel] Telephone Company in these words : * Weather unfavourable ; postpone your visit.' I just wish to draw the attention of the House to the fact that the Bell Telephone Company, an organization brought into being by this

House, and protected by its charter, has such a loose way of carrying on its operations as under certain circumstances to cause serious consequences. It appears that Lord Dundonald placed confidence in the message delivered by that company. I realize that this being a private matter, there is no claim. I just wish to draw the attention of the House to the position in which the Beil Telephone Company stands in relation to the public of Canada. I may say that when the true condition of affairs was realized, His Lordship immediately ordered a special train to convey him to Alexandria, and the celebration took place as it was originally planned.
Motion negatived.

speechtext:
1 have had placed in my hands in the last half hour a telegram, and I would like to draw the attention of the acting Minister of Railways and Canals to its contents, and request him most respectfully to inquire into it. It is as follows :
Niagara Falls, Ont., September 7, 1903. E. F. Clarke, M.P.,
House of Commons, -Ottawa.
Railroad fare for Yankees from Niagara Falls, N.Y., to Toronto and return, one dollar and fifty cents ; -railroad fare for Canadians from Niagara Falls, Ont., to Toronto and return, two dollars and fifty cents. Bring this up in the Ho-use land ask if it is right when they are trying to put the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway through. I will vouch for this.

I would be obliged if the hon. minister would make inquiries to ascertain if it is possible that this discrimination in rates between passengers from the same place and over the same system takes place.
Do I understand that that is on the Grand Trunk Railway ?
Yes.
I shall be very glad to have it inquired into.

Before the Orders of the Day are called, as I now see the Minister of Agriculture in his place, I desire to say that I took occasion yesterday to refer to an interview which took place in Toronto, given by Mr. W. T. R. Preston, Commissioner of Immigration in London, to the Toronto ' News,' in which he spoke in a manner not at all complimentary to a very important agricultural product. I had hoped that the minister would make some statement with a view to lessening the mischief which I think
was calculated to be done by the statement made by Mr. Preston.
If the hon. gentleman wishes to put a question to the government, he cannot make any statement.
I will move

That cannot be done. I may say, with respect to these questions which are put when the Orders of the Day are called, that they are not quite a regular way of proceeding. At the same time, l suppose that questions at such a time may lie allowed, but they should be put as questions and without comment.

If you will permit me to proceed, I will confine myself to a question. But it will be necessary for me to draw the attention of the minister to a further despatch under ' Canadian Associated Press ' which the minister will find in the ' Citizen ' of this morning. I would ask if he had inquired into the matter and purposes taking any steps with a view to removing the slander that, I think, has been
placed upon Canadian butter-
The hon. gentleman should not
Of course, not a slander by any member of this House.

That is not the point. But when a question is asked before the Orders of the Day are called, the rules applying to questions should be observed. The question should be a question purely and simply and should not contain any statement of facts.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) has put the question as to whether the Minister of Agriculture has looked into the matter referred to in the paragraph indicated. As it was only yesterday that the paragraph came to the government's attention, I have had no opportunity of doing so. speechtext: This clause came up for consideration some time ago. We thought it better to put it over, to consider whether it was advisable to pass it or not. This was adopted, as I explained, from the New York Penal Code. The object is to make provision with respect to men engaged in the active militia who are called out in time of strike. 1 propose to fill up the blanks in this clause, with regard to the fine, with the words ' not exceeding fifty dollars and not less than ten dollars.'

That section seems to go a long way. Here are two clauses A and B. A contains the words ' deprive any other person of his employment ' and B the words ' or prevents any other person from being employed by himself or another,' while C has '.obstructs or annoys any other person or his employer in respect of the trade, business or employment of such other person, because such other person is an officer or man of the active militia, and so on. These terms are very broad, and would take in every labour organization trying to enforce the rights of its members. Does the minister think that subsections A and B are controlled by these words ' because such other person is an officer or man of the active militia,' as C is ?
Of course.
It did not strike me so when I first read it.
I cannot see any doubt about it myself.
Has that first section been taken verbatim from the New York statute 7
I would not like to say it is absolutely verbatim, but it lias been drafted for the purpose of conveying my own ideas.
We have the New York Act here ?
It is in the library. If my hon. friend desires to have this section stand over, I am willing' because there is another section that I want to ask to stand myself.
I would like to have it stand. Does the Minister of Justice know whether it has received any judicial interpretation in New York?

I do not know how old the New York statute is, but it has been in force there for a couple of years. I would not consider it important whether a judicial construction has been put upon it or not, provided it conveys our own ideas.
As I read it, I have great doubt whether (a) and (b) are controlled in any way by (c).
The hon. gentleman will notice that the word ' or ' runs through the sections, and it is governed by the word1 ' because.'

At the first reading, it seems to me you have to introduce a very nice construction to get (a) and (b) controlled by (c). I am afraid the courts will say that parliament has not a nice literary idea in drawing these clauses.
Section 75a allowed to stand.
On section 198a-amending section 205,

This was introduced at the request of the Royal Art Union of London, with the laudable desire of distributing works, of art. But since the section has been introduced, representations have been made to me that it is liable to open the door again to the inconveniences that have resulted from lotteries established heretofore in Montreal. I have endeavoured to point out that this amendment will not produce that effect, but those who are interested in the good work carried on against lotteries seem to think it is liable to have a damaging effect upon their work in Montreal. Consequently, I think it is better to allow that section to drop for the present.
On section 257a,
Is this instead of the Bill introduced by the hon. member for Montreal, St. Lawrence, (Mr. Bickerdike) ?

I would not like my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) to say that it is instead of it, or in substitution for the Bill introduced by my hon. friend for Montreal, St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike). This is a little attempt at legislation on my own account. I am sorry to say that the legislation I have introduced does not appear to satisfy any person. I have had protests from all over Canada from the Women's Christian Temperance Union to the effect that this legislation does not go far enough. On the other hand I have had protests from other quarters to the effect that this legislation goes very much farther than is necessary under the circumstances. In view of that I sacrifice this section to the protests of both parties and let it go at present in the hope that next year I may be

able to do something better. This can go as a peace offering to both factions.
Does the hon. Minister of Justice expect next year to be able to do anything better in the way of satisfying the people ?
I thought if I took the middle course that it would satisfy both parties.

Is it not the best test of your proposal that both sides complain ? Though not an extremist, I think something should be done in the way of controlling the cigarette smoking habit in reference to boys of a certain age. I do not know what should be the limit, but I think that the adoption of a provision of this kind is good policy. We should not be entirely controlled by people who send us telegrams. We ought to make up our minds what is right and do it. I think the horn minister had better let it stay as it was at the beginning.

I regret very much that the parties who sought for prohibition would not accept this excellent step in the direction of what they asked for. I am very much surprised that there should be any objection raised by the Women's Christian Temperance Union against this legislation because it is a firm step in advance. While I would not say that such a thing as prohibition is going to effect a cure, I think that as a deterrent this will be found to be an excellent piece of legislation. I am sorry that the hon. Minister of Justice has permitted these letters to affect him. I know his equable legal temperament and he might say that viewing the question from this side and that, he might better drop the whole thing. I would say that any correspondence that would bring about the result of dropping this section would only seem to indicate that those who had asked for it had permitted their better judgment to run away witli them.
Not their better judgment, their worse judgment.

I put it that way because they are ladies

their better judgment. I must be gallant. I can only say that a great deal of good will result from this legislation and I do not know how we could get at lit in any better way than in the way which is proposed. I never believed that by saying cigarettes shall not be manufactured or imported we were going to prevent anybody from smoking cigarettes, but I say to those who are interested in preventing boys from smoking cigarettes that a great deal will be accomplished by legislation of this kind. I regret very much that those reformers, who are among the salt of the earth, the best people in Canada, should have done what reformers very often do, namely, if they do not get all they want they will not accept that which is in their best* interests.
Do they object to this clause ?
Yes, that is the trouble.
They want it made stronger.

I think in view of that fact the hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) is acting wisely, if the people in whose interest this clause is prepared will not accept it. It must be borne in mind, too, that a great deal of pressure has been brought to bear on the hon. minister by people who claim that the clause he has prepared is too drastic. A large delegation of persons engaged in the tobacco business came down to interview the hon. minister hnd they also interviewed a great many members. They pointed out that they did not open up tobacco shops for the purpose of selling cigarettes to minors, and that if the clause which the hon. Minister of Justice inserted in this Bill were permitted to pass it would work a great injustice to them. They recognize that the evil is one that should be grappled with, and what they suggested was that the clause should stand for twelve {months and that in the meantime both parties in the matter should make representations to the hon. Minister of Justice in the hope that one that would more nearly commend itself to both parties could be adopted.

This clause has just the fatal objection which was urged against the Ontario Act. The Ontario Act provides against the selling of cigarettes to minors under 10 years of age. The way the Act is evaded is this :	A number of boys will
congregate in some place. One or two of them will be over 10 years of age and the rest of the boys will give their money into the hands of the boys who are over 16 years of age who will buy the cigarettes and distribute them amongst their companions. The raising of the age limit by two years or more will not prevent that from being done in future as it is done to-day and I do not wonder that the Women's Christian Temperance Union object to it.

We should not be deterred from passing good legislation such as this because it will be evaded in certain directions. I cannot assume that in all cases you will And boys who are ready to do what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) suggests. I admit that boys will have as many little ideas in their heads as to how to evade this law as grown up people, but the fact that this law will be on the statute-book will act as a deterrent and an educator. It is a good deal that the boy will know that it is upon the statute-book. The country is full of good boys who smoke cigarettes without perhaps knowing that it is not a good thing for themselves, but the fact that the boy will know that what he is doing is not only not good for himself but that it is not legal, will have good effect. I regret

that the Women's Christian Temperance | Union did not accept and accept gratefully this step which is a step in the right direction.

I think this is a very important and strong section, notwithstanding the fact that it draws an objection from the Women's Christian Temperance Union of Canada and the tobacco manufacturers.
I know, speaking for Nova Scotia, that they represent the very best class of people down there. I do not know what they may represent elsewhere but the Women's Christian Temperance Union represent people who are not cranks but who are anxious for the preservation of their families and who are desirous of promoting those objects which every woman and mother ought to be interested in. I agree with the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) thoroughly that this is a step in the right direction and I believe so on two grounds. First,
I believe it will deter the ordinary dealer from selling to a boy. because such an Act would impose upon him a heavy penalty. Secondly, I agree with the argument of the hon. member for Guysborough. that once a boy understands that the smoking of cigarettes under a certain age is illegal, unless he is a very bad boy, he will be deterred. Once he knows it is illegal to smoke cigarettes, once he knows that if he goes along the street with a cigarette in his mouth he may be reported to a law officer he will be encouraged to abandon the habit. The sellers of tobacco are respectable men, they do not want to be subjected to prosecution for selling to a minor and to be liable to the penalty under the law. Therefore, you reach the boy who wants to smoke the cigarette ; and you reach the man who sells cigarettes.
Now, while I am not an extremest in any of these ways, yet, I cannot but recoguize the facts, as I see them. I have observed, on the streets of the town of Truro, young boys, of thirteen and fourteen, smoking cigarettes ; and, in every case, they are degenerate looking, emaciated, pale-faced ; and I have no doubt that this is due to their having acquired this habit. No doubt, this habit is striking at the manhood of the country, equally with the drinking of liquor. Therefore, as everybody ought to be anxious that the strength of the country should be preserved, we ought to preserve young boys who might, from want of warning, and before they understand the value of strength and intellectual and physical power, destroy themselves, through this habit. For these reasons, I think this is a moderate section. I would ask the minister not to bow to every telegram he may receive. from interested parties, either from the Women's Christian Temperance Union, or from the cigarette people. They are interested parties. We are the judges ; we should sit here as competent men, listen to both the one side and the other, and decide the question. We should be prepared to say, this is right and fair, or, you are extreme in Mr. FRASER.
your views, you ask too much we cannot get the public opinion of Canada to go so far.
I am prepared, for one, to say to the minister, that I support this measure. Whatever may be the contention, on either side, this is a step in the right direction. If, later oh, we find this is likely to do good, we can go further. This section should be preserved.

While this clause does not go so far as the original legislation proposed, I certainly think it should be allowed to stand. I had some conversation with the ladies of the Women's Christain Temperance Union, having been the seconder of the original resolution.
Oh, oh.

I am willing, at any time, to be again the seconder of a similar resolution. I was not the only member of the House who had an interview with the ladies. I fancy all the members had that pleasure. In conversation with them, after the original Bill was thrown out, I tried to persuade them to accept this as a half-way measure. I do not know what objections to it have been presented to the minister, but I believe that the mass of reformers-I mean reformers in the sense of those who are trying to reform this evil-will be satis-fled with this, as far as it goes. For my part, I would prefer something more drastic; but, failing that, I think reformers would be willing to accept this as half a loaf.
I would urge upon the minister to allow this to stand. The very fact that this is a Dominion law, that the force of the Dominion is behind it, will have a good effect in prevent the selling of cigarettes to boys. I would be glad to see the age limit raised a little further. When we had the discussion, I saw that notice had been given of a measure in the British parliament to provide that no tobacco in any form be sold to boys under twenty-one. I have no objection to the section now under discussion, so far as it goes, but my own preference would be to have the age limit raised. I think the minister would conform to public sentiment if he would allow this section to remain part of the Criminal Code ; I am sure it will receive the endorsation of the great bulk of the people who favour legislation of this kind. It may not meet the views of the Women's Christian Temperance Union. But if this legislation is not provided, they will probably come down to the House next year and ask for legislation similar to that which was thrown out. If this is enacted, it may anticipate that. While I favour the prohibition of the sale of cigarettes, 1 recognize that there are great difficulties m the way of such a measure. But, I am satisfied that a clause of this kind will be effective in accomplishing good, and I hope the minister will allow it to stand.

I wish to add my word to what has been said by the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley) and the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser).

This legislation is in the right direction. Too many young lads are in the habit of smoking cigarettes, and any legislation that [DOT]will have the effect of decreasing this practice is in the right direction. Therefore, I should be sorry if the Minister of Justice found it necessary to abandon this clause. I am not sure that the clause as framed is the best for the purpose, but it is a move in the right direction, and, if it is not found to be exactly right, it can be amended.

When the resolution of the hon. member for Montreal, St. Lawrence, (Mr. Bickerdike) was before the House I took strong ground against it, because I believed, that if carried into law, it would not have the desired effect. I do not believe that public sentiment in this country would back up such a law if put upon the statute-book, that is, a law prohibiting the sale of cigarettes to any persons in Canada. Rut the present section, it seems to me, is a step in another direction, and in the right direction. I do not think anybody would charge me with being a crank on this question. But representing, as I do, a constituency whose people take a serious interest in this matter, I can only enter my protest against this section being withdrawn. It would have been far better, if this section is to be withdrawn, if it had never been put in the Bill. It is rather an indication to the people that we are afraid of the legislation, and it does not seem to me that that would have a salutary effect, so far as the boys of our land are concerned. I am not speaking here with reference to the tobacco habit. Probably a great many of us would not be very consistent in speaking on that subject. But I am here to say that I believe the smoking of cigarettes by boys is one of the worst evils we have in this country to-day, especially in the case of boys from fourteen to sixteen years of age. I would point out that we have upon the statute-books of a number of the provinces, a law similar to that here proposed. I would only ask the Minister of Justice, if he cannot see his way clear to allow this section to be voted upon, or at least to allow it to stand. It would be a step backward to withdraw the section, now that it has appeared in the Bill.

I desire to add my protest also against the dropping of this clause. Nor am I satisfied altogether with the reasons given for the dropping of it. The fact that the two contending parties in respect to this legislation both object to it, would, under ordinary circumstances, lead one to believe that possibly, a very fair clause had been provided. I am not prepared to say, speaking for myself, that I would legislate more drastically than it is proposed to do by this clause. But, inasmuch as this is a clause which we have had under consideration. I simply desire to state that I am prepared to support it, and i 337
I protest against it being dropped. As the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) has stated, similar clauses exist in the statute-books of the provinces, not, perhaps going quite so far. But I do not think it can be urged that this goes too far and I hope it will be enacted by this parliament.

I think it would be a very grave error for the Minister of Justice to allow this clause to drop. I am satisfied that the effect on the people who inaugurated the movement against the sale and manufacture of cigarettes would be rather injurious. It would have the tendency to keep them from all similar good work in future to give them no law at all. This parliament has done nothing in the direction indicated by the motion of the hon. member for Montreal, St. Lawrence ; and now, when we have another opportunity to pass legislation in connection with this matter, apparently it is to be withdrawn. I think that would not be right. We all know the hurtfulness to children and to growing boys, of the use of tobacco in the form of cigarettes. During the present session of this parliament, it has been shown that the smoking of cigarettes by boys is extremely injurious to them. Under such circumstances, it is right and proper that we should adopt such legislation as this. In my opinion the clause as it stands is better calculated to answer the purpose we have in view, than the proposal which was submitted to the House earlier in the session. Cigarettes are so easily made, that it is questionable whether you can possibly prohibit their use by law. It is very easy to buy the cigarette paper and the cigarette tobacco already cut, and consequently, boys can very) easily make their own cigarettes. Such being the case, cigarettes would be largely used by certain people who would make them themselves, and in this way, no doubt the revenue would be affected. However, I believe that the legislation contained in the clause now before us, would have a deterrent effect, and in that respect it is a move in the right direction.

I for one would be very sorry indeed to see this clause stricken out of the Bill. We all remember what a very large majority there was in favour of the prohibition of cigarettes, when the proposition was first submitted to this House, and if we cannot get all that we actually want in the matter of prohibitory legislation, we can perhaps get some legislation which will be beneficial. If this clause is going to be stricken out of the Bill, I suppose we cannot help it ; but next session we will have to begin over again, anl re-introduce the Bill which this session was ruled out of order because of some irregularity in the form of its introduction. I had occasion recently to speak to a number of people in my own town in reference to this cigarette evil, and my information is that the evil



is growing worse and "worse amongst the boys who attend our collegiate institute. Last week when I was in Toronto, the ladies of the Women's Christian Temperance Union came to me to talk about the nature of the legislation which they expected might be passed this session.
I explained to them the provisions of this Bill, and they stated that if such a Bill were passed it would be a step in the right direction, and, that as they could not get all they asked, this provision would perhaps be ample for the time being ; at all events they would be able to see how it would work in practice. I shall regret very much indeed if this clause be allowed to drop. If It is dropped, then we shall have to renew our efforts next session.

I believe that this clause is in the right direction, and I join with the other hon. members in raising my voice against dropping it from the Bill. In fact, Sir, I think the provision in this clause is better than the provision in the original Bill, because it strikes at the root of the evil, and will provide a remedy.

I wish to add a word to what has already been said by hon. gentlemen, as to the evils which result from the use of cigarettes by boys under the age of eighteen. We have it on the authority of physicians, that the use of cigarettes by young boys is most injurious. These physicians, wlio are our very best guide in such a matter have expressed themselves in no unmeasured terms in regard to the matter. I believe that the use of tobacco in any form is injurious, but, when indulged in by young men it is peculiarly harmful, in that it leads to other ills, which in the course of time become uncontrollable. I appeal to the government not to withdraw this legislation, because I believe it to be a step in the right direction. If I had my way I would recommend that the age limit be placed at over eigh-een years, because if youths were prohibited from using cigarettes until they were twenty-one years, then when a young man attained his* majority he would be better able to judge for himself between right and wrong and he would no doubt feel -the more strongly that he was committing a very serious offence, should he break the law by smoking cigarettes. If we had such a law upon the statute-book, the community of any particular locality would no doubt be interested in enforcing that law for the sake of the good name of the place. Some few Sundays ago, on my way to church, I saw three or four youths who were not more than fourteen or fifteen years of age, smoking cigarettes on the street. I spoke to them, and pointed out to them the evil they were doing, and I took the cigarettes from them. One of them pouted a little at my action, but I felt satisfied that not only had I done an act of justice to the boys Mr. WRIGHT.
themselves, but that I had given a good example to others.

I regard this clause in the Bill we are now considering as an exact copy of the Ontario statute. We have had such a law in the province of Ontario for a number of years and I am not aware that any harm has resulted from its operation. I believe that that law has been beneficial, and I am quite sure that no one in the province of Ontario would desire to see it repealed. The hon. gentleman from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) said that the Ontario Act only extended to the age of sixteen years, but on reference I find that the age limit is there specified at eighteen years, just as in the clause under discussion. I trust that the Minister of Justice will allow the clause to stand as part of the Bill. Even if it be not the law in the other provinces, outside of Ontario, I am quite sure we will make no mistake if we extend the Act to the whole Dominion. I cannot understand how, by dropping this clause, the Minister of Justice will meet the wishes of the ladies to whom he has referred. As I understand it, these ladies requires more drastic legislation, and if the Minister of Justice cannot meet their wishes at present, I think it would be a very proper thing to allow the clause to stand, in order that the other provinces of the Dominion may reap from it the benefits which we are now enjoying in Ontario.

I wish to say to the Minister of Justice, that in view of the recent decision of the Privy Council on the Lord's Day Act, probably all similar provincial Acts may be dead, and therefore this clause should be passed in order that the country may have some substantial protection against the cigarette evil.

The weak point in this clause is the fact, that it does not go quite far enough. My hon. friend (Mr. Gour-ley) seems to think that this clause made it illegal for a lad to smoke a cigarette, but as a matter of fact the clause only provides that it is illegal to sell cigarettes to youths under the age specified in the clause. If this clause went a little further, and made it illegal for * boy under eighteen years old to be seen smoking cigarettes on the streets, or anywhere else, then more good would be accomplished. Such a provision would certainly have an educational effect. The Minister of Justice should not only retain this clause in the Bill, but he should make it still more stringent by providing that it would be illegal for a boy under a certain specified age to smoke cigarettes.

I endorse the view of my hon. friend (Mr. Rosamond!. I feel satisfied that if the law gave authority to any person who found a boy smoking cigarettes, to take him in charge and pass him over to the authorities, it would have a much more beneficial effect.

That may be just exactly the way we will not get legislation-by wanting everything at one time. This legislation goes fairly far ; let us accept it. There are a hundred and one things we would like to see in operation, but we cannot have them, as they are unworkable. Ret us test one thing first ; that is the education people get in law, and then the other thing will come more easily. We cajnnot go this far without calling for something more.

I would like to state the reasons why I came to the conclusion which I have just mentioned. There is considerable conflict of opinion in this country on the subject of tobacco legislation. There a re those who think that the manufacture and sale of tobacco ought to be prohibited absolutely. There are others who think that this question of prohibiting the use of tobacco by persons of a certain age is more a matter for parental control-a matter that ought to be regulated by the parents in each family. These are the two extremes. Between these two extremes there stand the moderate men, who think that this cigarette business has got to be a very serious matter-something that ought to be regulated by the state. 1 say regulated designedly, because I do not think we ought to go too far in the direction of state control over the conduct of children, or of adults either. But in respect to this particular matter, there are those moderate men who think that we ought to regulate so as to prevent what is, in the minds of some people, at all events, a nuisance. Hence the legislation that was introduced by my hon. friend from Montreal, and which went in the direction of prohibiting the sale and manufacture of tobacco. Those who are supposed to be anxious for that particular legislation are dissatisfied with the middle course which I have proposed. and which is embodied in the section now under consideration. There are others who wish to see this trade regulated, and who think this provision does not go in>
the right direction for that purpose. For instance, there are those who make representations to the effect that if this legislation passes, it will work gross injustice to those honest traders who merely desire, after all, to carry on an honest calling, and that it will have the effect of creating a gang of informers who will seek, by tempting children, to create trouble for those who would not otherwise be interfered with in carrying on their business. My idea was that this legislation, not going far enough to meet the wish of either party, we should drop it, with the view of having the whole matter re-considered, and bringing in other legislation at a future time. I think myself, after having heard the representations on both sides, that this section can be improved. I do not wish to do that hurriedly.
337J
I have given an earnest of my good intentions at all events ; on further consideration, I hope to be able to draft a clause which Will be free from the objections urged on both sides to the clause under consideration, which either goes too far or does not go far enough.

I wish to enter my objection to the withdrawal of this clause. My hon. friend from Halton has pointed out that it is a fac-simile of the clause in the Ontario law. I understand that that is very generally acceptable, only the law is not enforced in that province. I do not think the passage of this clause now would in any wise prevent further legislation with, reference to the sale and manufacture of cigarettes in this country. I understood this clause to be a compromise between the extreme views held on either side of the question. For myself, I wish to enter my objection to the withdrawal of it, and to say that I think it should pass at this session of parliament; and if the government, on consideration, think it advisable to bring in further legislation, it can afterwards be submitted for the consideration of the House.

It is understood, of course, that I drop this clause for the purpose of re-introducing another clause, which I think will better meet the real necessities of the situation. I am not going to allow myself to be influenced too much by those who are interested in the sale of cigarettes, nor on the other hand, by those who think that because they do not smoke themselves, nobody else should do so. I wish to introduce legislation with reference to the use of cigarettes by children.

Will you introduce it this
session ?
That is my intention-before this Bill goes through committee.

Would the minister be prepared to say now whether he would consider it an offence against the law for children to be found on the streets smoking cigai

ettes ?

That is a very proper suggestion, and it is in reality the idea I had in my mind as to how far it was proper to punish merely the man who sells under a mistaken notion as to the age of tine person who purchases, and allow the child to go scot-free. As the parents of this country appear exceedingly anxious to suppress the cigarette, I think we ought, if possible, to reach the parent through the child.

I think tine Minister of Justice, in considering legislation for the future, should consider that policy. The

parents should lend a hand to help to carry out the law.

I ought to say this, in addition, that I have received, I venture to say, over a hundred protests from the Women's Christian Temperance Onion all over Canada against this legislation, and I have not heard a voice raised in favour of it except what I have heard hene to-day.
Section 257 struck out.
Progress reported.

House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Act respecting the Judges of Provincial Courts ; and to provide that the salary of the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of the Northwest Territories shall he $5,000, and of five puisne judges of the said court, each, $4,000 per annum.-The Minister of Justice.

This resolution is introduced for the purpose of providing for the appointment of two additional judges. The salaries are not changed. Very strong representations have been made by the bar to the effect that there are not sufficient judges at present in the territories. For the present we take power to appoint an additional one.
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick).

speechtext: Why not send up some of the Ontario judges instead of sending them perambulating around the country on commissions ?
That is a valuable suggestion, which possibly may be considered when making the appointment.
Has the hon. minister anything to show that the legal business before the courts has greatly increased.

It has increased enormously both civil and criminal. I know more perhaps about the criminal business, because it is under the direct control of the Department of Justice. The criminal business has increased over fifty per cent in the last two years.
Four years ago, I was living in the North-west and it was hard to get a judge to go on circuit, so that I can quite understand that the increase is called for.

Does the hon. minister consider $5,000 sufficient salary for the chief justice of the Supreme Court of the North-west Territories ? Living there is much higher than the east and for a posi-Mr. GILMOUB.
tion of that kind you should have the ablest lawyers. I hardly think that any leading lawyer would give up his practice to accept the position.
He will have no practice to give up.
Such men should not get the position. It should be given to the ablest lawyers. Five thousand dollars is hardly sufficient.

There Is a great plenty of game there and any amount of beef and sheep and it ought to be quite easy to live upon $5,000 per year.
Resolution reported,
House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
1. Resolved, that the salaries of the judges of the Supreme Court of Judicature of Ontario
shall be as follows :-
Per annum.
The Chief Justice of Ontario	$6,000
Pour Justices of Appeal, each	 5,000
The Chief Justice of the King's Bench.. 6,000 Two judges of the High Court of Justice,
King's bench division, each	 5,000
The Chancellor of Ontario	 6,000
Two judges of the High Court of Justice,
chancery division, each	 5,000
The Chief Justice of the Common Pleas 6,000 Two judges of the High Court of Justice,
common pleas division, each	 5,000
The Chief Justice of the Exchequer
division	 6,000
Two judges of the High Court of Justice,
Exchequer division, each	 5,000
2. Resolved, that if the Chief Justice of the
King's Bench, the Chancellor of Ontario, the Chief Justice of the Common Pleas, or the Chief Justice of the Exchequer Division, is appointed to the Court of Appeal, the Governor in Council may direct that he be paid a salary not less than that previously enjoyed by him as such chief justice or chancellor.-The Minister of Justice.

Charles Fitzpatrick). This is introduced to bring our Dominion legislation into line with the Ontario legislation. By the Ontario Judicature Act, amended last June, it is provided that there shall be an Exchequer Division of the high court, which makes it necessary to provide for a chief justice and a puisne judge for the new division. The court of appeals is not affected by this resolution at all.

I congratulate the legislature of Ontario in having found this means of increasing the salaries of the judges in that province. I hope that the legislature of the province of Quebec will take a leaf out of the Ontario book and pass a similar law and thus increase the very insufficient remuneration paid to our judges in Quebec. In that province there are two chief justices and one acting chief justice-the chief justice of the Court of Appeals, the chief justice of the superior court and the acting chief justice of the superior court, who

lives in Montreal, when the chief justice lives in Quebec, and vice versa. In Ontario, under the new Bill, there are five chief justices, each receiving a salary of $6,000. I find also in resolution number two a very good way of increasing the salaries of the judges, because it provides that if a chief justice of one of the divisions is appointed to the Court of Appeal, although under the law he should receive only $5,000, the same as the other puisne judges, he continues to receive $6,000. There are fourteen judges in Ontario, who receive a salary of not less than $5,000, and live who receive a salary of not less than $6,000. And there may be judges appointed to the Court of Appeal, who had been chief justices of the lower courts, and they will also receive $6,000. I would like again to call the attention of my hon. friend, as it has been often before, to the utter insufficiency of the salaries of the judges in Montreal. It is not because we who belong to the learned profession wish to become judges that we urge an increase in the salary, but because we believe that we are really doing a service to the country by bringing this question to the attention of the authorities time and again. I can quite understand that it is not the fault of my hon. friend if he has not been able this session to bring before the House a Bill increasing the salaries of-the judges in Toronto, in Montreal, and in Quebec. I would not advocate at the present time an increase in the salaries of the judges generally all through the Dominion. But if he consults anybody who knows anything about the cost of living in the city of Montreal, he will be told that the sum of $5,000 is absolutely inadequate for a man occupying the high social position that a judge should occupy in such a city as Montreal. All business men in the city of Montreal will tell my hon. friend that, not only those who are connected with the legal profession, but those who have anything to do in the business circles of that city. It seems to me extraordinary that a man having in his hands the administration of justice, a man who very often has to determine, not only upon the life and death of an individual, but upon his fortune to the extent, perhaps, of hundreds of thousands of dollars, should receive the paltry sum of five or six thousand dollars, while a man who is at the head of a financial institution, perhaps a small institution, receives a salary of $10,000, and while others who are at the head of great corporations receive salaries of from $25,000 to $50,000 a year. I may say that in Montreal the judges are precluded from accepting any civilities from anybody, or any of the amenities of social life, because they are absolutely unable to return them. As I said before, this question has occupied the attention of the House several times. I can understand that at this late date of the session it would be impossible to bring in a measure, what I
would call a measure of relief ; and I would again urge upon my hon. friend-he is a strong man in the government, he has a great deal of influence in the government and with the supporters of the government- and I would suggest to him that now is a good occasion to make a change, if not this session, at least next session-if we have a next session-I do not want the right hon. gentleman who leads the House to commit himself upon that question now ; but if we have another session of this parliament, I hope he will heed the views of the great majority of the people in the province of Quebec and of the Dominion at large, and bring in a measure by which the salaries of the judges will be increased to a figure somewhat adequate to the high functions they have to exercise, and the high social position which they occupy in this country.

I wish to call the minister's attention to what appears to me an . anomaly in the different salaries provided for in this resolution. The salaries of the Court of Appeal judges are the same in the resolution as those of the high court judges. Perhaps the minister will tell me if I am mistaken, but I think the judges of the high court have allowances that the Court of Appeal judges have not, circuit allowances and things of that kind. So that in fact, from what appears here, a judge of the high court does really receive a higher remuneration than a judge of the Court of Appeal. Now it strikes me as rather singular that a judge of the high court should receive a lesser remuneration than the judges of the Court of Appeal, who are the judges of the highest court in the province, and who decide appeals from the other courts ; yet they receive lesser pay, a lesser remuneration, at all events, than those over whom they rank. I would also like to point out to the minister that for the salaries mentioned here. $5,000 for a puisne judge and $6,000 for a chief justice, you cannot persuade the best men at the bar to take seats upon the bench. I think it is generally conceded throughout the province-it is a question that one does not like to discuss very fully, because it might appear to reflect upon those who have been appointed and are now sitting upon the bench-but there is no question, I think, that the government cannot obtain the services upon the bench of the best men at the Bar in Ontario, for the salaries that are mentioned here. I think that is a subject the government should take up and deal with, for it is notorious that the very best men cannot be obtained at present, and it should be possible at all times to put upon the bench of the province the very best material that the province affords.

I am disposed to agree with my hon. friend that we cannot secure the best men at the Bar to

take seats upon the bench when they are paid such inadequate salaries. Of course I am speaking now as Minister of Justice, and cannot take a different position from that in the Bill, while speaking as a private member I would probably have something else to say. With respect to the judges of the Court of Appeal, my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) will bear in mind that the judges of the high court receive what is called circuit allowances when they go on circuit in different parts of the country, and receive thereby additional remuneration. My hon. friend will know better than I, but I understand that the judges of the Court of Appeal also go on circuit sometimes, and then they will be entitled to the same remuneration as is paid to the ordinary high court judge.
I think they do not hold circuit now, they did some years ago.
Circuit allowances are paid really to judges of the high court who go on circuit.

I would ask the Minister of Justice to explain the difference between the salaries of the judges mentioned here. For instance, we have county court judges in Ontario who get $2,400 a year and travelling expenses. I do not find in the other provinces judges who correspond with them. The salaries I think are higher in most of the other provinces. In Manitoba, the North-west Territories and British Columbia there are no travelling expenses allowed, and I presume those expenses are provided for otherwise. I would like the Minister of Justice to give us a general outline of the differences, and why they exist.

In the province of Quebec we have no county court judges at all, in consequence of the judicial system that was inaugurated before confederation. Under it all the judges were appointed as members of what we call there the superior court. The courts in our province are divided into the superior courts which are courts of original jurisdiction, and the Court of Appeal, to which appeals are taken from judgments of the superior courts. In Ontario you have a different system ; you have your high court judges, your judges of the Court of Appeal, and your county court judges, and that system,
I believe, exists in all the English speaking provinces. I am not quite sure that the system of county court judges, such as they have it in the English-speaking provinces, is not an advantage over the system we have in our province. I think if we were to change the system in our province and appoint county court judges, it would be an advantage. We have no power to do it here. But speaking as a member of the Bar of Quebec, I may say that I think if we were to reduce the number of high court judges and appoint county court judges, I Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.
who would perform somewhat similar duties to those now performed by county court judges in Ontario, the system would be improved. Some years ago when I was a member of the local legislature, I had occasion to discuss a Bill of that sort introduced by the then Attorney General, and although we were on opposite sides of the House, I had to give my approval to the measure, because I thought that on the whole we had too many high court judges in Quebec. However, we have the system, we are not responsible for it, and all we can do is to conform to the requirements of the province in that respect. There is no remedy here, because the organization of the courts in that province is under the control of the provincial legislature. An hon. gentlemen near me suggests that our system costs less than that of Ontario ; I am sorry to say that I have to differ with him. As a matter of fact, in the province of Ontario the cost of the administration of justice is 12-320 cents per head ; in Quebec it is 13-24 cents per head, so we are somewhat more expensive. In Quebec it is to be expected that we should have more expense, because we have the dual language. Dealing with the particular question the hon. gentleman put a moment ago, I would say that county court judges are on the same footing as to salary and travelling expenses in all the provinces of the Dominion. County court judges in Ontario receive a salary of $2,400 and they get travelling expenses. The same thing applies in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Manitoba and British Columbia. In the territories they have no county court judges.
Does that scale apply to junior county court judges ?
Yes. The junior county court judges begin at $2,000 and their salaries increase annually to $2,400.

By the Auditor General's Report there does not seem to have been anything paid for travelling expenses in Manitoba. British Columbia or the Northwest Territories. That is what I was asking the hon. minister.
I have not the figures for this year hut for the last year for which I have figures I can state the result to my hon. friend. In Ontario there was paid for travelling expenses of judges $15,038.26.
That is in the Auditor General's Report What about the other provinces ?

I am going to give the hon. gentleman the statement for the other provinces. For Nova Scotia, the travelling expenses of judges amounted to $1,400; New Brunswick, $1,200; Prince

Edward Island, $584.94 ; Manitoba, $2,850.55 and British Columbia, $8,670.90. In respect to British Columbia and Manitoba, no distinction is made in salaries between the high court and county court judges and I cannot therefore give the amount in respect to each. In the North-west Territories the travelling expenses of judges amounted to $2,609.90.
Is that the total amount for each province or is that the amount that each judge received ?

In the province of Ontario the travelling allowance of high court judges is included in the circuit allowance. The circuit allowance for high court judges in Ontario amounted to $13,400 and the travel of county court judges amounted to $15,038.20. I omitted to say that in Nova Scotia the cost per capita is 11-52-100 cents.
I would like to ask the hon. minister why the travelling expenses I have referred to do not appear in the Auditor General's Report ?

Perhaps my hon. friend did not look in the proper quarter. I cannot give the information to my hon. friend because I did not prepare these figures. They were prepared for me by the accountant of the department and I will hand them to my hon. friend so that he can have them verified if necessary.
If the hon. minister will turn to page M-15-16 of the Auditor General's Report he will find that there are no travelling expenses entered there.
The allowance made by the province of Ontario of $1,000 to each judge who goes on circuit, would make up the $13,400 that the hon. Minister of Justice lias referred to.

I am not talking about Ontario at all ; I am talking about the other provinces. If the Minister of Justice will turn up the Auditor General's Report at the pages I have referred to he will see that there is nothing in the report at those pages in reference to travelling expenses. They must have had travelling expenses and there must be some way of explaining the omission.
The amounts I stated are the amounts taken out of the accountant's books in the Department of Justice and the figures show the amounts actually paid out by us in respect to these different items.

Will the lion. Minister of Justice get the explanation and give it to the House why these figures do not appear in the Auditor General's Report ? I think we have a right to that information. If the hon. Minister of Justice will turn up
page M-15-16 he will see that these tra-^ veiling expenses are not given.
If my hon. friend will look at page M-8 he will find the accounts for circuit travelling of judges authorized by Supply Bill.
For which province ?
Manitoba, Ontario, and on the preceding page, the North-west Territories.
It is strange that part of it should appear in one place in the Auditor General's Report and that the statement for other places should be left out.
I am afraid I would meet with a very cool reception if I were to offer any suggestions to the Auditor General as to the way he should make out his report.

I would like to ask the hon. minister whether there is a separate circuit allowance for judges in the province of Ontario going upon circuit irrespective of the amount they get for travelling expenses ?
No, the circuit allowance covers the travelling expenses.
How much is it ?
I think about $1,000 a year.
Is that paid by the Dominion ?
It is under the Dominion statute.
And in Quebec the travelling expenses for judges are $6 per day.
Yes.
While actually travelling.
While actually travelling.
That makes quite a difference between the two provinces.

The system is very different, in our province a judge who does his duty-but perhaps that is too harsh a term-'would have very little travelling expenses because he would live in his district and his travelling expenses would only include the cost of going on circuit within the limits of his district. But, in regard to our Court of Appeal I introduced an amendment to our statute in respect to the payment of travelling expenses to our judges on the Court of Appeal, who, I thought, ought to be paid at least the amount they receive. At all events they are

content with what they receive at the present time.

Is it not a fact that in the province of Ontario the province pays to each judge who goes out on circuit $1,000 a year ? I am afraid we are getting the thing mixed. It may be that the Dominion allows each judge $1,000 extra for expenses, but I think there is $1,000 allowed by the province of Ontario to each judge and that is $1,000 that the hon. minister refers to.
There is in addition to his circuit allowance paid by us to each judge the amount that is paid by the province of Ontario.
Which is $1,000.
And I understand that the $1,000 paid by the province of Ontario is applicable to all the courts there.
No, only to the trial judges, only to those who go on circuit.

I think the chief justice of the Couit of Appeal also gets it. However, my hon. friend will probably know more about it than I do. By our legislation, instead of paying travelling expenses, there is circuit allowances to judges of the high court but that does not apply to the Court of Appeal.

I understand the difference between the two provinces is this : In the province of Ontario every judge of the Superior Court, gets either $(>,000 or $5,000 a year, lie gets $1,000 from the provincial government and he gets $1,000 from this government which would make in the case of tile five chief justices $8,000 and in the case of each puisne judge, $7,000 each.

The chiefs get $7,000 in the province of Ontario as the result of the payment made by the province. They get $6,000 in addition to what the province gives them and the puisne judges gets $5,000. In addition to that instead of getting travelling, expenses they get a circuit allowance. I can tell my hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) that I could mention judges in our own province who get more than that as a result of their travelling expenses.
There are very few.
There are one or two who are very great friends of both of us.
In Quebec there are three judges who gets $6,000 a vear and the other judges in the cities get $5,000 a year while the judges in the rural parts, I suppose about ten of them, get $4,000 a year each.
With us ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: Yes, except there are two. who get $3,500 a year, one for the district of Chicoutimi and Saguenay. There is really a great difference between the remuneration accorded to judges in Ontario from one source or another, and the remuneration which is accorded to the judges in the province of Quebec. It is true that when judges travel in the province of Quebec they get $6 a day, but this allowance, in a good many instances, is far from meet- -ing the requirements of the case. I know of some judges in Montreal who have to go on circuit in the counties of Soulanges and Vaudreuil, and it costs them certainly more than $6 a day to pay their travelling fai;es and hotel expenses.

One of the reasons why judges in Ontario get more than judges in Quebec, is due to the fact that the local legislatures pay the Ontario judges $1,000 extra. If the judges are not paid enough in the province of Quebec, we have no objection to tl>e legislature giving them $1,000 more.

Does the Minister of Justice think that the second paragraph of this resolution is advisable? It grants to a chief justice promoted from the common pleas division to the Court of Appeals the same salary as he had before promotion. That would present a very great anomaly. You would have judges of very unequal salary among the puisne judges of the Court of Appeal, and one of these puisne judges might, in fact, have the same salary as the chief justice himself. I myself am against the principle of promoting judges from court to court. I believe that when thiey accept a very high position such as a seat on the bench, it should be upon the understanding -very rarely departed from-that they would remain in that position. It makes them more independent, and I think it gives to the public greater guarantee of their independence. But in case a chief justice of one of the superior courts should be promoted to a puisne judgeship in the Court of Appeals, he should abandon his claim to the salary of $6,000, and he should be put upon the same footing as the other puisne judges of the Court of Appeals. I cannot agree with what has been said, that the acting chief justice, for instance, at Montreal, and, the chief justice who sits in Quebec, should not receive a greater salary than the puisne judges of the Court of Appeals. They are all courts of high jurisdiction. and the chief justice of the lower court has a great deal more to do than tlie puisne judges of the Court of Appeals.
It is quite natural that, under these circumstances, the chief justice of the superior court should receive a larger salary, 'fhe point I have raised as to section 2 of this resolution should commend itself to the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice.

Subsection 2 of section 3 of tbe Act amended, is a distinct inducement which has been held out for a number of years to the chief justices of the different subdivisions of the High Court of Ontario, but I may say to my hon. friend that no chief justice has ever yet agreed to go to the Court of Appeal, notwithstanding that he might receive the additional salary. I agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) in what he has said about the undesirability of promotion on the bench. I think the old English rule : once a puisne judge a puisne judge for ever, is a very good rule. Whien a man goes on the bench, it is not a bad thing for him to feel that he is like the man who enters that place that Haute speaks of ; and that he leaves all hope of preferment behind him. and all hope of reward, either directly or indirectly, from any source whatever. He should only hope for the satisfaction which comes to him from performing his duty. However, that is my personal view, and perhaps it is not necessary for me to express it. If my hon. friend from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) looks at chapter 138, section 13, R.S.C., he will find that an Ontario judge, instead of getting a travelling allowance of $6 a day, is allowed $100 for each time he holds court on circuit.
At one o'clock. Committee took recess.
Committee resumed at three o'clock.

I want to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Justice to a grievance which we have in Nova Scotia. We have not many grievances down there ; we are a very contented people ; but at the same time our judges have for many years felt that there was an Invidious distinction made between Ontario and Nova Scotia, and between Ontario and some of the other smaller provinces. I hold that there are no provinces in Canada as far as the administration of justice is concerned. Canada for judicial purposes is divided into territories called Nova Scotia, Ontario, &c. In these different territories those who exercise the highest judicial functions ought to be all treated alike. I think we put an impress of inferiority upon a judge who exercises the jurisdiction of the highest court of the country, by paying him a smaller salary than others who exercise the same jurisdiction, simply because he happens to exercise it in a smaller territory. Our judges have complained again and again of this invidious distinction. 1 claim that a judge who exercises the highest jurisdiction in his territory, no matter where that territory may be, ought to be treated in just the same way as any other judge who exercises the same jurisdiction in another part of the country. I desire to emphasize that, because it lias been the cause of complaint for many years. Another complaint in Nova Scotia is made on behalf of the county court judges. These
judges are very able men, who would discharge the functions of the Supreme Court with ability equal to that displayed by the Supreme Court judges ; and the idea of asking men of education and of high intellectual qualities to accept $2,400 a year and exercise high judicial functions is what cannot longer be put up with in Canada. As between the salaries of the Supreme Court judges in Nova Scotia and those of the county court judges, if only one or the other could be increased, I think we would all concur in saying that it should be the salaries of the county court judges. The $2,400 paid to the county court judges, even with the travelling expenses of $200 thrown in, is very much less than the $4,000 paid to the Supreme Court judges with their circuit allowances. We have Judge Morse in the county of Cumberland, a very able and distinguished man. He preferred to take the county court, because he had a large estate to look after, and did not care to go to Halifax. It is a shame to offer $2,400 for the ability which he brings to bear on his judicial duties. He is a man of great literary ability, and an able man in every department of life, as well as a lawyer and a judge. I have letters from several of our county court judges asking me to represent this matter to parliament. To offer these men so insignificant a sum as $2,400 is very like the outrage of offering members of parliament an indemnity of $1,500, which I regard as the supreme outrage of the country. One other point, to which I wish to draw attention is, that our county Court judges have had thrown upon them important functions under the County Court Judges Criminal Act. Some of these judges are only county court judges by name. They do not sit for one county merely ; they sit for a district composed of three or four counties. The province is divided into seven districts. For instance, the district in which I live includes the counties of King's. Hants, and Colchester. The judge for the district happens to live at the other end, Kentville, in the county of King's. When any person is thrown into jail in the county of Colchester, the sheriff notifies the judge, and he is compelled to come and hold court. For that he receives no travelling expenses or additional salary. His travelling fees are entirely in connection with the civil branch of the court, which is held only twice a year in my county.
I think my hon. friend will remember that the county court judge gets $200 for travelling expenses.

That is for the civil end of the court. At any rate, the petty salary of $2,400, with the small travelling fees included, is utterly inadequate remuneration for a judge. All of our judges have protested, and have written to us asking us to bring the matter before parliament. I had

a letter from one of the judges the other day, saying that he did not wish to complain, but that to be called away to travel over two counties once a week or once a fortnight, and to be compelled to pay his own expenses, was unendurable. A judge-may have to hold ten or twenty of these courts in the course of a year. Therefore, 1 hope the Minister of Justice will give these judges an addition of $600 or $1,000 to their salaries. Nothing would be more fair or just.

I regret -that the minister did not go further, for while he is providing an increase of salary for the judges of the Supreme Court of judicature in Ontario, iirmy opinion the county court judges are as deserving of an increase of salary as the high court judges. It has been the subject of general complaiut for many years that the county court judges have been very poorly paid. Representations have been made to the Department of Justice more than once, with the object of having some readjustment made in accordance with the requirements of the situation. It is an undeniable fact that the cost of living has increased in late years, but for many years there has been no increase in the salaries of the judges. While the earning powers of everybody else have increased, the earning powers of the judges have remained the same as before, though their expenses have increased like the expenses of other people. I know that many of the judges find it difficult to make both ends meet, and to -maintain that respectability which judges should maintain. X do not know why this government is so reluctant to take this matter up and deal with it. Several times we have had intimations that they intended to do so. The Minister of Justice is dealing with the salaries of a few of the judges ; but why not go on and deal with them all-the county court judges as well as the high court judges ? It seems to me that no one could be selected better qualified to do this than the present Minister of Justice, because he seems to have the courage of his convictions ; and when he makes up his mind to do anything, he goes on and does it. Therefore, I see no reason why he should not take up the whole matter, and increase the salaries of the judges all along the line.

When legislation was introduced in the Ontario legislature last session to provide for the appointment of two more judges, it was very fiercely opposed, as it deserved to be, by the opposition in that House, and particularly by Mr. J. J. Foy, whose respectability and attainments in the legal profession give weight to his opinion. In Ontario we have ten judges who go on circuit-four in the chancery division, three on the King's Bench, and three in Common Pleas. Of these ten judges, four were on leave of absence a
good part of the time and out of the country, so that practically all the work was done by six.
Only three were absent.

One would imagine from the travelling expenses of some of them, that they must have been travelling all the time. I think there were four, but in any case three were absent the best part of the year. Where therefore is the necessity of appointing two more ? This government is not to blame for the legislation passed by Ontario, but so long as we keep on increasing the number of Superior Court judges, so long will that increase be a bar to the increase of the judges salaries in that province. Under this arrangement, one of the judges is to be withdrawn from the Court of Chancery and two more added to make up the so-called Exchequer Division. The result will be that while six, or, at the most, seven judges did the work last year, you are going to add two more, and as some of these who were absent last year were unfortunately either removed by death or are going to resign, the work which last year was done by seven last year will in future be done by twelve. The people of Ontario understand what the duties of the Supreme Court judges are. Year after year, in a large county like Simcoe, jurors were summoned and came twice a year at great expense to the county, but as there was not a single case for trial by jury they were not required. That got to be such an abuse that a Bill was introduced by Mr. Hoyles which practically does away with jury, by providing that notice shall be published some time before the court opens, if there be no criminal case that will require the intervention of a jury. In my opinion, the salaries of the Supreme Court judges should he increased. Under this Bill $0,000 are allowed them. Under an Ontario statute mother $1,000 is allowed them-and then there seems to be an allowance of $1,000 a year to each one for travelling expenses. BjUti a reference to the Auditor General's Report will show that while some of the judges of the Superior Court spent only $1,000 on travelling others were paid $2,000 and $1,700 and $1,400 and $1,500 and so on. Assuming that a judge is assigned to Toronto and another one to Brampton-the latter is an old county where the court rarely sits a day or two-one would think that a very small amount would cover the travelling expenses. There are besides local sessions held at Ottawa and London, in connection with which there would be some travelling expenses. What the public would like would be to have this allowance for travelling expenses done away with altogether and the number of trial judges reduced to nine, giving the Chief Justice $10,000 and the puisne judges about $8,000 per year. In the Auditor General's Report, we find one gentleman drawing $2,000 in

expenses, in addition to his regular salary as a judge. It is to he regretted that the Ontario legislature saw fit to appoint this extra number of judges.
How many ?
Two.

Who pays them 7
Mr. BENNETT The federal government must make the necessary financial provision. Once they are appointed by the local legislature, the federal government supplies the sinews of'war. I know that there are gentlemen on the bench who could easily earn $10,000 per year at their profession-men of very eminent standing-and if you are going to draw on the bar for extra new judges, you will not, unless you increase the salaries, have as good a class of men on the benches as you have had in the past. As regards the county court judges I disagree with the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule). I believe that they should be paid a .fair salary, but it is notorious in Ontario that in some counties, where there are a junior and a senior judge, there are practically no cases to be tried all the year around. Litigation is not as extensive in Ontario as it was some years ago. I can recall, when I was a student at law, seeing the assizes court last in Simcoe forty days, whereas now it is through in a week, and I think that that statement applies to Ontario all through. There is less work. True there has been a certain amount of congestion in the appeal courts of Ontario, but this does not help the appeal courts at all. We are simply appointing two new judges to go on circuit. I regret that the province of Ontario has introduced legislation appointing new judges; but as it has been introduced, this House has only one thing to do and that 'is to fix the salaries.

I might say to my hon. friend from Grey (Mr. Sproule) that this does not propose an increase in the salaries of the Ontario judges. My hon. friend (Mr. Bennett), in mentioning the congested condition of the Court of Appeals, gave a reason for this Bill. The result of this amendment will be to provide for two divisions of the court of appeals.

Are we to understand that the three judges composing the Exchequer Court will sit in review on cases taken to appeal from the King's Bench or the common pleas or the old chancery division ? Or are they not to be circuit judges ?

Every circuit higb court judge may be called on to sit in appeal. As I am not familiar with the procedure in the province of Ontario, I think it will be safer for me to read the section of the Act, section 5 :
Section 12 of the Judicature Act is hereby repealed and the following substituted therefor: -
12. (1) In case from pressure of business, or
other cause it shall at any time seem expedient to the Lieutenant Governor in Council or to the judges of the Court of Appeal or the judges of the Supreme Court of a majority of them (of which majority two judges of the Court of Appeal including the chief justice, unless absent on leave, shall form part) the Court of Appeal may sit in two divisions either at the same time or at different times.
Then, it proceeds to make provision for the selection of judges to sit in two divisions of the Court of Appeal. So, the appointment of these judges will enable.the Court of Appeal to sit in two divisions ; and, in that way, besides doing ordinary circuit work if called upon, they may sit as a division of the Court of Appeal.

There are five judges in the Court of Appeal, and if you add three, as undier this proposal, that would make eight; then, if you make two divisions, they could not be an appellate court, there being an even number of judges.

That is not the way it is intended to proceed. These judges will not have exclusively the right to sit in appeal. Any of the judges of the High Court will have the right to sit in appeal. There will be practically twelve judges who will have that right. As I understand the system in Ontario, four judges form a quorum in the Court of Appeal. So, when the court sits in two divisions, having eight judges they will have the necessary number to form a quorum in both of the two divisions. My hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) speaks of the travelling allowances. I cannot understand very well how it is that the sums which my hon. friend mentioned have been paid to these officers, because the statute makes provision that, in the province of Ontario, each of the judges of the high court shall be paid $100 for travelling allowance for each time he holds court in any county except the county of York and the city of Toronto. So, the only explanation of the very large amount that appears in the Auditor General's report as having been paid to the judges would be that, possibly, the judges sat in connection with election trials.
They get paid $200 a piece for each election trial.
Yes, they would receive that in addition. Except for this, all judges receive the same for all courts-$100 for each sitting.
Who pays them for the weekly courts 7
In addition to that there is the weekly court, which, I believe, they hold exclusively in Ottawa and London. They are paid $6 a day each for travelling expenses in connection with these courts.

I have been listening with some considerable interest to the discussion

in connection with the increase of superior court judges' salaries. I hare heard gentlemen here say that those appointed to the Supreme Court judgeships are gentlemen who are earning very large salaries. I am not in a position to speak for other portions of the Dominion, but I know a little about the state of affairs in the province of Ontario; and the number of lawyers in Ontario who are earning $10,000 or more a year are very few. There is no use in men standing up in this House and saying that they can ; the fact remains that they cannot and do not earn such large salaries in the province of Ontario. When hou. gentlemen stand up In this House and say that the people of the province of Ontario are in favour of increasing the superior court judges' salaries, I beg to differ; and I say that, in my opinion, the people of the province of Ontario particularly are opposed to any such increase of salary. Looking over the record, 1 find that once, if not twice, since confederation, and notably in the year 1873, there was a Bill presented in this House, by which the county court judges' salaries were decreased, while the superior court judges' salaries were increased. I am of opinion that if there should be any increase of salaries given by this parliament to any judges of this country, that increase should be given to the county court judges. I am firmly convinced that the superior court judges of this country are well paid. And I repeat that it is all very well for hon. members to stand up in this House and state the contrary. I know that there is a sort of affiliation between members of the bar on this subject. I understand that well, and the bar should remember that the public understand it very well, to. The people know how much importance to attach to the general discussion that goes on between members of the bar in this House and outside of the House-a sort of mutual admiration society, as my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) says. Take the average man in every calling in this eouu-try at the present moment, and, I have no hesitation in saying-and I want to speak fairly, because I think the judges should be well paid-that there is no class of people in this country better paid than are the superior court judges at the present time. It is all very well to point to some gentleman occupying a high position in a railway company as receiving $25,000 or $50.000 a year. That is all very true; but his salary has to be paid by one corporation. We are dealing with the general public, and with the public's money. For my part. I think it is about time, notwithstanding the general prosperity of this country, the surpluses and all that, that parliament should come to the conclusion that a time will come in the history of this country when we shall have dissatisfaction on this subject and the surpluses will disappear, and when somebody will be asking that
