these salaries be reduced. I think it is time that members of parliament should discuss this question in a way that would meet the wishes of the electors of this country. I want to say for myself, I am very much opposed to an increase in the superior court judges' salaries. If the salaries of any judges are to be increased, the increase should go to the judges whose salaries were decreased in 1873, when the Act to which I have refererd was passed in this House.

I do not happen to belong to the legal profession, but I must say that my attention has been drawn, again and again, to the salaries paid to the junior judges of the county court of the county of York. If men are paid at all, they should be paid according to the work they do. I have drawn the attention of the hon. gentleman who is now Minister of Justice, as I drew the attention of his predecessor, to the salaries paid to these junior judges to Whom I have referred. 1 think that if a re-arrangement of salaries is to take place, especially in the province of Ontario, the junior judges of the county of York, because of the immense volume of work that they do year after year in that county, are entitled to consideration. With regard to the salaries paid to superior court judges, I think that it is in the public Interest that the men who occupy distinguished, honourable and responsible positions sliouldi be men above reproach, and should be paid adequate salaries. That is what should be aimed at. You may have too many judges, but those who occupy these distinguished positions should be paid ample salaries. I think it is not to the welfare of the commonwealth that the judges should be obliged, as they are sometimes, to supplement their salaries by going on boards of different mercantile institutions or acting on commissions. I would support any reasonable increase of the salaries of judges in the province of Ontario and, of the Dominion, provided I am assured that we have not more judges than are necessary to do the work within a reasonable time. If it is germane to the discussion, may I ask the Minister of Justice if an amendment has been made concerning the salaries of the junior judges of the county of York? I think it is fair to say that it is impossible for those gentlemen to live and maintain the position they should maintain, in the city of Toronto, on the salaries they receive. They are paid, I believe $2,000
They have the distinct advantage over other judges that, from the time they are appointed, they are paid $2,400.

But the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) knows that the cost of living in Toronto has substantially increased in the last few years, and the business these gentlemen are called upon to discharge lias very substantially increased.

Inasmuch as I entirely dissent from the way in which the hon. member for Peel has read public opinion in the province of Ontario, I feel it my duty to speak, notwithstanding that I belong to the ' affiliation ' which the hon. gentleman alleges, exists at the bar. However, it is pleasing to know that the feeling of the bar on both sides of the House and of a number of the laymen, is a unit on this question. I think that if you polled a vote in the province of Ontario the conclusion come to would be that the judges of the province are not paid sufficiently.
Not a bit .of it.

1 may be wrong, but I, think so. At all events, I am not afraid to say, and I represent a rural constituency, that the salaries now paid to judges, and which were fixed some twenty-five years ago, are no longer sufficient. They were then put in a position where they could live in a manner befitting the dignity of their position ; that is no longer the case. It is ridiculous for any hon. gentleman to say that judges with salaries of $5,000 or $6,000 a year, living in Montreal, or Toronto, or Halifax, or Winnipeg, can maintain that social position that a judge ought to maintain, because they cannot. The price of living, it is admitted, has increased by 30 or 40 per cent. Now if that be so, is it not in the interest of every citizen of Canada that the judiciary should be placed in the financial position which they occupied originally when these salaries were fixed ? It is in the public interest that men who are appointed to the bench should be placed in a position where they will not be beholden to any one, where they will be perfectly independent, where they will not have to look elsewhere to obtain that monetary assistance which will enable them to maintain the dignity of their position. Now, unless you put them in that position, I would almost go as far as to say that it is a menace to justice, because you cannot obtain men who will be in that independent position that the judiciary of this country should occupy, unless they are made absolutely independent from a monetary standpoint. Now, if this increase was made it would be a small tax upon the rate-payers of this country as compared with the taxes they are called upon to pay in subsidizing the large enterprises which we are subsidizing every session of parliament. As I have already said, when the salaries were fixed originally twenty-five years ago, $5,000 or $6,000 were considered very large salaries according to the incomes then earned by leaders of the bar. It was a fair income, and in fact one that any leader of the bar at that time would have been glad to accept. Now, notwithstanding what the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) said, I think that salary is not one quarter of the sums that leaders of the bar in the various
provinces are able to earn to-day. It must be remembered that these gentlemen have to decide cases of enormous importance, involving hundreds of thousands of dollars, yes, millions of dollars ; and how can men decide such large causes in an independent way unless they are assured of an independent means of living? It is a well known fact that at the present time you cannot get the leaders of the bar in either Ontario or Quebec to accept judicial positions. That is not so in England, because there they are always able to get the best talent for the bench, it is the ultimate goal of every leader of the bar in England, because they "are paid such salaries as enable them to accept that position and to maintain the dignity of the judiciary. But in this country, I regret to say, you have not been able, for the past ten years, to get the leaders of the bar, at least in the two great provinces I have mentioned, to accept judicial positions. That is a sweeping statement, I may be told. Doubtless we have isolated instances of leading members of the bar who have accepted judicial positions. But in the majority of instances, if a position is offered upon the Supreme Court of Canada, or upon the Supreme Court of either of the provinces, it is refused, or rather'the Intimation is given that if the position was offered it would not be accepted. I know that to be a fact, and I do not think that the citizens of this country desire that state of things should continue. I think it behooves us as members of this House to see that the members of the judiciary throughout the Dominion of Canada are placed in an independent position, where they will be able to maintain the dignity which befits gentlemen occupying that high position, where they have to try causes involving hundreds of thousands, and millions of dollars, as well os the liberty and the life of individuals.
The committee need not ask to what profession my hon. friend belongs.
That is a small criticism.
I am not discussing this question from a small standpoint at all. I am just as liberal in my views as my hon. friend, who lives in the city of Toronto and represents a rural constituency.
That is a small criticism too.

I could easily make a personal reference if I wished, and if my hon. friend is not more careful, I will do so.
I think I know something about the feelings of the electors, particularly in the province of Ontario, as well as my hon. friend does ; and when he stands up here and says that the cost of living has increased from 30 to 40 per cent over what it was twenty-five years ago, I beg to differ with the hon.

gentleman. I desire to say, Mr. Chairman, that there is no article of living that enters into the ordinary household of this country but what can be bought cheaper to-day than at any time during the last twenty-live years. My hon. friend laughs-it is all very well to try to mislead the people, but the facts remain the same. There is not a man at the bar who cannot buy his clothing cheaper than he could twenty-five years ago ; there is not a man at the bar who cannot buy his boots and shoes cheaper than he could twenty-five years ago; there is not an article on the hoh. gentleman's table to-day that he cannot buy cheaper than he could twenty-five years ago. The only exception to the rule is in the case of house rent, which, in the province of Ontario, is greater than it was twenty-five years ago. Would the hon. gentleman pretend to tell his electors that is not the case ? The electors of this country understand that subject well. The difficulty, Mr. Chairman, is, I think, that some of these gentlemen on the bench have gone into an advanced system of living, they want to live in a style above that of other people who help pay the taxes.
I know as much about this as the hon. member for North Simcoe ; and I say that the mem at the bar in the city of Toronto who are earning $10,000 a. year and more, are very few. Take the smaller cities of Ontario, take Hamilton, London and Brantford, and you can apply the same remark to the smaller towns and villages where there are many distinguished lawyers who are earning salaries less than those proposed to be given to the judges. I come from a town myself where we have lawyers that would take a high position on the bench anywhere in this country, and I know what they are earning in that county, and my hon. friend knows it too. I say that there are splendid lawyers all over the province of Ontario, in every city and town, that are not earning one half of $8,000 in their profession, and yet they are men who would adorn the bench of this country. Have we come to this in Canada that judges will only dole out justice according to the amount of salary they receive ? Are we to understand that because the judges are not well paid, in the opinion of these hon. gentlemen, they are not now giving the people justice on the bench ? Is that the position? I do not understand that to be the position myself. I have a high regard for the judges of this country, and I do not wish to say anything disrespectful of that honourable body ; but I say that it is time that the members of the profession both in this House and out of it, should understand that the salaries of other gentlemen who are working just as hard, and who have as much ability, are not advancing at the same ratio that this Bill proposes to advance the salaries of the judges of the superior* court. I would challenge my hon. friend to go into his county, let him go be-Mr. BLAXN.
fore his electors in the next election, and say that he is in favour of increasing the salaries of the superior court judges, and let him look out for the electors of that county, because they know as much about this matter as the hon. gentleman himself.
1 do not wish to make any personal references at all, and will not. I am talking from a broad standpoint, and I say that I can find men in this House and out of this House who were occupying positions just as responsible, who require just as much ability to discharge their duties as the ability that is required to discharge the duties of the superior court bench, and who receive half the salaries that are paid to the judges. The time has arrived in the history of this province when the lawyers in the different towns and cities earn less than they earned fifteen years ago. There is no use pretending to say that people are being offered these judgeships and that they are refusing them. We understand that very well. The public are not misled by statements of that sort.
Does the hon. gentleman refute the statement that several lawyers have recently been offered positions on the Supreme Court bench of several provinces and have refused them V

Mr. Chairman, I feel that I ought to say a word about this question. I am a layman, and it is the laymen who will have to pay the tax imposed by the increase in the salaries of the judges. Therefore, the layman should be consulted. The argument against the contention of the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy) is that when a judgeship becomes vacant in any of the counties there is no lack of applicants to fill the position. I was told a few moments ago by a friend that he knew where they were tumbling over each other to get the job in his county. If that is so, the hon. minister need not have any trouble about getting men to fill these positions. I have some regard for the taxpayer as well as the judges. My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) has illustrated his case very well. He says that the cost of living nowadays is not very much higher than it was twenty years ago. I know that to be the fact. Judges need not wish to occupy a higher plane than the rest of the people. They wish to be independent. I do not think the hon. Minister of Justice will find it necessary to increase the salaries of judges in order to induce members of the legal profession to accept positions on the bench.

I remember very distinctly that during the first parliament in which I had the honour of being the representative of Lennox, when the late Rt. Hon. Sir John A. Macdonald was leader of the House and, of course, leader of the government, he introduced a Bill to raise the judges' salaries. It kicked up quite a hubub all over the House, and when we had a caucus over it about thirty of the back bench members stood out against it, with the result that we heard nothing more of the Bill.
You heard something of it when Sir John Thompson was Prime Minister.

Sir John Thompson did not succeed either, and I do not think the present government will succeed, and if they do they will hear from the country. We have a vacancy in Lennox, at least we had- it may be filled now. The county judgeship is vacant, and we had all the lawyers on one side of politics down here looking after it. and all the other fellows on the other side would have been glad to get it. The salary is $2,400 a year and travelling expenses. My hon. friend from North Sim-coe (Mr. McCarthy) says you cannot get the leaders of the bar to take these positions. I do not think that the leaders of the bar could get them if the salaries were higher. I do not accuse these hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches of being much worse than their predecessors in this regard, but we all know that the men who have the influence get these positions, and sometimes they are not overly well qualified.
Not always.

I said generally. I did not say always. If my hon. friend from North Simcoe will go up to the county of Lennox and take the ground which he has taken here to-day I should he very glad, or if he will get the man who opposes me, if I have the honour to be the candidate in the next election, to take that ground, it will be an easy job for me. The people of this country believe that the judges are being well enough paid for all they have to do, and that they are being well enough paid for all they will have to do for a long time to come. I think there is another feeling prevalent in the country, and that is that we have too many of them. We all know that in the smaller centres, and I presume that in the cities it is quite as bad, from year to year the profession is getting more and more crowded, that lawyers are making less and less money, and that they are glad to resort to things that are sometimes not in keeping with the dignity of their profession to make a livelihood. Many men of good ability have to do these things. I am well acquainted with the lawyers of my town, and I regard them as a very respectable lot of men, but I do not know a single one of them who would not be glad to get a county judgeship at the present salary.

I agree with what the hon. member for Lennox (Mr. Wilson) and the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) have said. I do not approve of a present increase in the number of judges in Ontario. I think the judges who are there are capable of doing the work, but I did not think they are paid properly. I think they are very much underpaid. Let me ask these hon. gentlemen if the position of a chief justice or of any puisne judge is not as responsible as that of a railway commissioner under the Railway Commission Bill ?
It may be as responsible in many ways as the position of manager of the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Grand Trunk Railway, but one would not expect to pay the judges as large salaries.

No, because the standard has been kept down. There are more of them to be appointed, but you do not pay judges one-tenth of the amount that you pay the managers of the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Grand Trunk Railway, and the responsibility is almost as great. But take the gentlemen whom at this Session we thought ought to be put in the position of railway commissioners, and whose position is no more responsible than that of a judge, if it is as responsible. One of the responsibilities that they are relieved of is the trying of a man for his life. That is the greatest of responsibilities ; yet, this House has voted that the chairman of this commission should receive $10,000 and that the other commissioner should receive $8,000. What was the argument which led to

that salary being fixed at $10,000 ? It was- notwithstanding what the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) says-that the cost of living generally has advanced in the larger cities.
Mr. CASGRA1N. Hear, hear.
So far as rent is concerned there is no doubt about that. The incidental expenses have Increased by 30 or 40 per cent, the cost of living to gentleman occupying the position of high court judges.
Would my hon. friend allow me to ask him a question ? Would he be good enough just to tell us the items of the increased cost of living in the city of Toronto ?

The difficulty in deal-' ing with that is, that one has to enter into the personal affairs of judges to a certain extent. I can tell my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) that when the first chief justice of Ontario was appointed, on the salary he received he was able to keep two or three servants, and he was able to keep horses and a man servant. If you compare the price of labour twenty-five years ago with what it is now, and the cost of street car fares, and telephones, and a hundred and one other things
Might I ask the hon. gentleman, if they pay street car fares, do they have to keep horses as well ; do they ride in both at the same time ?

Certainly they do not ride in both at the same time, but if you live at a certain distance out of town you have to get into town, and street cars must be used if a horse is not available. The more one argues this with my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) the more it is apparent that the hon. gentleman does not understand the basis on which the argument is made as to the 30 or 40 per cent increase in the cost of living. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) would disagree with me on that, and I am quite content to agree to disagree with him. This same argument which enables you to fix a salary for a railway commissioner, should apply when you are fixing the salary of a high court judge. I say in all sincerity, that I think any one judge of our high court has a more responsible position to fill than the railway commissioner, and if that be so, then the salaries of our high court judges should be commensurate With that responsibility.

It is rather amusing to hear a lawyer of the standing of the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCarthy) talk as he does about the judges. He talks about the responsibility of the position of a judge, and compares it with that of a railway commissioner, but it is a different kind of responsibility. If you take all the judges and lawyers in Canada to-day, you perhaps would not get a good railway commissioner out of the
Mr. McCarthy.
whole lot of them. There are only two or three men perhaps on the continent who could manage a great railway, but there are a great many lawyers who think they could make judges.
No.

Yes, it is all very well, to talk about the responsibility of judges ; but what do judges do ? You take a six thousand dollar judge who has a good many perquisites besides, and you have to get twelve men at two dollars each to see that justice is done. And then you talk about the responsibility of the judges. I would rather have those twelve men dispense justice, than any judge you have on the bench-There is never a man who wants fair-play who does not want that twelve common sense hard-headed men should try him instead of a judge. When the trial is going on you have all the lawyers, and all the paraphernalia, and you have the judge ; but a comon sense community of average ability will have justice meted out by twelve men before the court can arrive at a verdict. A judge is not supposed to be valued by a mere money value. Is there nothing in the position outside the money a judge gets ?
I thought a man should be guided in such a high position, not by the pay he draws, but by a sense of honour and respect for the position in which he is placed by the country. There should be a fine sense of duty guiding a judge, far and above any money consideration. Why, Sir, if the government would elevate men to the bench who are as big as the salary, we should have better judges than we have to-day. We have judges on the bench to-day who could not earn six thousand dollars a year In the practice of their profession. It is said that the expense of living has increased. Let the judges economize as the rest of us poor fellows have to do and they will find their salaries sufficient. You cannot make a seven yards suit out of a six yards piece of cloth ; you must cut your suit according to your cloth. Let the judges do that once in a while and they will have a little sympathy with the poor accused who has to fight many a battle that the judge has not to fight. It would be well if a little more of the ordinary experience of life came to our judges, so that they would be better able to deal out justice to the commonalty. If they had a little experience of that kind, justice would be tempered with mercy. It is all very well to say that judges must have three servants, but what has that to do with the rendering of justice? We are told that a judge has got to have a carriage and two or three servants to see that he gets along the street without being injured. What has that to do with the carriage of justice in this country ? Street car justice-well, I do not want any justice on wheels so far as I am concerned. Why, the country is chock full of lawyers:

there are more lawyers to-day in this province than there are briefs, and it is time that the lawyers were put to some honest work to make a living. The judges in this country have got to suffer some inconvenience. 1 am quite aware that the position has a dignity about it that the judges ought to be in a position to maintain, but it is not necessary that they should roll in wealth to do it. A judge may be a man of a high sense of honour, and he may have the fullest confidence of the community without having a large bank account. The largest bank account is not necessarily followed by the highest honour ; not by any means. I notice that men who are prospective judges are very anxious to have the salaries placed at a high figure. I suppose that the members of this House of Commons are very sorry their predecessors did not raise the indemnity away up to 82,500 a year. In the same way these prospective judges are anxious to have the salaries raised so that there will be no trouble when they get to the bench. There are hard worked judges in every county, travelling about on their circuits, who are perhaps underpaid to a greater extent than are these gentlemen mentioned in this Bill. They ought to have some consideration. By the plan adopted in this province-and I might as well talk about it as a layman-you cannot do any law business unless you have an agent up in Toronto. The whole legal business of the province virtually centres in Toronto, and you have to get a fellow up there to go to the hall, to get an order to do so and so, and so and so. That has been going on in this province for years, and the milch cow has gone dry on the poor fellow out in the county. The whole business is being done in Toronto, and they want to measure up the salaries the judges shall get by the incomes received by some prominent, special men the number of whom you can count on your fingers. I am aware that every man in the profession, when he gets old. has to suffer, the experience of younger and more vigorous men passing him in the race, and perhaps the profession to which I belong is the only one in which that experience does not occur because you can go out into the fields and view four fields and your flocks, and feel that they are your own. Let the judges do as other people do ; let them live within a reasonable income, and they will get along. If there is anything that the judges of the courts and the lawyers should do, it is to teach the people true economy. If they did that, there would be fewer criminals in this country. But they teach them the other view of life, which is a distorted view, and hence the crime. I do not know that there are worse abettors of crime in the whole country, when you come to look at it. I think we should start right here, and do like the men who said that the Lord would send them a preacher, if he was 338
only religious, they would pay him a salary to make him humble.

A few weeks ago, when this resolution was introduced to the House, I ventured briefly to express my views on the question, and since then I have given the matter considerable thought, and have consulted not only with judges and gentlemen in the profession, but also to a greater or less extent with the people generally. I have found no reason, since I spoke on this question last, to alter my opinion as then expressed. I do not intend now to repeat what was said then, or to advance any argument in favour of increasing the salaries of the superior court judges ; nor do I intend to argue that their salaries are now large enough. But I want to take occasion to point out that the principle upon which the county court judges have been dealt with is by comparison, altogether unfair to them. As my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) has already pointed out, at the time of confederation the salaries of the superior and county court judges were fixed, and the duties of their offices assigned. The duties then imposed on the superior court judges have not since been increased. They have the same duties to perform to-day that they had to perform then, with this qualification, that the population and the wealth of the country have increased, and consequently there is more business for them to perform. But instead of their duties having been increased, their duties have been very largely decreased. At the time of confederation all the chamber business in the superior courts, such as motions for injunctions, mandamus, &c., had all to be performed by the judges of the high court in Toronto, and lawyers In the country had to send their business to Toronto to be performed by the judges there at the expense of their clients. The legislature in its wisdom has seen fit to alter that state of affairs by providing that chamber motions, and all interlocutory applications, in cases brought in a particular county, may now be taken before the county court judge of that county, who has been made a local judge of the high court. I think I am within the mark when I say that from thirty to forty per cent of this kind of work, which was formerly performed by the high court judges is now performed by the county court judges in the various counties. Now, as my hon. friend from Peel has pointed out, the salaries of the high court judges have been increased twice since confederation. By the Act of 1873, $1,000 was added to their salaries. bringing them up to $5,000 for puisne judges and $0,000 for chief justices. The Ontario legislature supplemented these salaries by paying them $1,000 more. So that their salaries have been increased twice since confederation. Their travelling, allowances have also been increased. They



are allowed $100 for holding each assize court, though it is a notorious fact that In most counties iu Ontario the judges open the court, dispose of the business and close the court iu two days, so that their actual expenses would perhaps be not more than $25. I am not saying that this is wrong, or that they are paid too much. But I want to call attention to the manner in which the county court judges have been [DOT]dealt with. At the time of confederation the salaries of the county court judges were fixed at $2,000, and they have remained at that figure until the Act was introduced in this parliament to readjust the salaries of the judges in 1813. The reason given in that Act for readjusting the salaries, as it was then put, is thus stated in the preamble of the Act : ' In view of the increased cost of living consequent on the diminished value of money, &c.,' the Act provided for increasing the salaries of the high court judges by $1,000. By that very same Act the salaries of the county court judges, to whom that statement applied just as much as it did to the high court judges, were reduced from $2,600 to $2,400. That was thirty years ago, and their salaries have remained the same from that day to this, although their work has been increased by more than 50 per cent. As I stated in my previous remarks on this question, since confederation there have been passed in the provincial legislature and in the Dominion parliament no less than fifty-two statutes imposing additional duties upon the county court judges, in addition to the duties imposed upon them by making them local judges of the high court. Now, if the cost of living was increased to the high court judges, it was certainly increased to the county court judges.
Then, there are a great many things which are deemed necessities to-day in the way of living which were scarcely known twenty-five or thirty years ago.	At that
time a coal oil lamp was the principal means of lighting houses; but today the electric light is a necessity. To-day electric light in one's house is a necessity. Thirty years ago we burnt wood at two and three dollars a cord, but now we burn coal which costs $7 and $8 per ton ? Thirty years ago we [DOT]drew water from a spring or river or well hut now we have water-works for which we pay taxes. Wages have increased and other expenses, but while there have been these increases in the cost of living, we find actual decreases in the amounts provided county court judges to meet those expenses. In addition to their salaries being reduced, their work has been increased over fifty per cent. They have now to do a good portion of the work formerly done by the high court judges. In many ways their earnings have been lopped off. Formerly the county court judges filled the office of master in chancery, to which certain fees are attached, but to-day we find very few county court judges in On-Mr. PORTER.
tario filling that office. That office is usually given to somebody else. Take the surrogate offices, which were formerly filled by the county court judges, to-day they are filled by others. It occurs to me therefore that county court judges have been dealt with unfairly, as compared with the high court judges, and the time is now opportune for the government to take the matter in hand and consider the whole question-not only the salaries of the superior and the county court judges, but the whole question of salaries. Let us adjust these salaries in such a way as to make them commensurate to the demands of the present day and the work to be done. It is not fair that gentlemen filling the honourable position of county court judge should be treated differently from those filling the position of high court judge. They should be treated fairly and paid a remuneration commensurate with the work to be done. Let any one sit down and figure out carefully, as I have done, what it costs a county court judge to live in a county town, and maintain the dignity of his office, and he will see that $2,400 is not at all adequate, taking into considera- * tion the rent, taxes, fuel, insurance, water-rates, light, and the support of a family, estimated at five, including clothing and education. There is another large expense which the county court judges had not to bear thirty years ago, but which they must undergo in order to keep up with their profession. They have to provide themselves with a library, the reports, periodicals, law journals, &c., which is no small expense. On a conservative estimate, a county court judge cannot live and enjoy the ordinary comforts of life on less than $2,200 or $2,300.
Is it fair then that he should only be paid $2,400 ? How is he going to provide for his family in the future ? He cannot engage in any other profession while oh the bench and should not do so, as he would thereby be lowering the dignity of his position, and he ought consequently to be paid, not only sufficient to enable him to live, but to enable him to lay by something for his family. That he cannot do on a salary of $2,400. I would urge on the lion. Minister of Justice to consider that view of fhe question and introduce legislation providing for a readjustment of the salaries of all the officials paid by the government. County court judges are not paid to-day as much as some of the officials of this government, who are not performing anything like as important duties or involving as great interests. I would suggest that the minister should introduce, at an early day. some measure that would give the relief to which county court judges especially are entitled.

I think there is a good deal in the suggestion of the hon. member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter) that this whole matter of the judges salaries in Canada should be seriously considered and perhaps. considered by a commission or a committee of this House. The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has spoken of the county court judges in the province of Ontario as receiving remuneration from other sources than the money appropriated for their salaries. That does not apply to Nova Scotia, though I do remember when the 3381
judges there used to be appointed revising officers under the late government. Now they are confined to the $2,400 of salary, and the few dollars of their travelling allowance. I do not think the point has been brought out strongly enough that the county court judges have increased duties. In the district in which I reside and practice my profession, from 90 to 95 per cent of the criminal practice of the district is before the county court judges under the Speedy Trials Act. The county court judges are not allowed any extra remuneration for this additional work. So, not only do 1 contend that the living expenses have increased very materially since the salary was made $2,400, but the judges' duties have been very materially increased since that time. I do not think we can attempt to deny the fact that living expenses have increased in the last twenty-five years. It is a fact that is patent to everybody ; it is patent to the people who demand higher salaries, including the artisans and workingmen. Even members of parliament have said that the expenses of living have increased so much that we felt justified in increasing our own salaries. Surely we cannot consistently contend that living expenses have liot increased during the last twenty-five years. No man can keep up the dignity of a county court judge and maintain his family as a judge should maintain his family, on $2,400 a year. Listening to this debate to-day, I hear hon. gentlemen say that the superior court judges of Ontario are paid salaries of $5,000, and that the judges of that province receive, including that which is paid to them by the Ontario government, between $6,000 and $7,000 a year. In Nova Scotia, I think, we have equally as good men upon the bench, but they are paid $4,000 a year, with $5,000 for the chief justice. Some hon. member spoke this afternoon about going to our constituents and talking this question over. I axn confident that I could go to my constituents or to the people of any constituency in Nova Scotia upon the issue of whether we should pay the judiciary decent living salaries, We can afford taxes in this country to pay for justice, but justice we must have. We must maintain the bench in a position of which we shall be proud. To pay only $4,000 to a Supreme Court judge, who is compelled to live in Halifax, where living expenses are high, is not reasonable. The salaries should be increased to at least $6,000 for the chief justice and $5,0(30 for the other members of the bench. Before I take my seat, I would like to ask the Minister of justice* if it is proposed, during the present session, to make provision in a case where a member of the bench becomes Incapacitated for his duties and remains so for a length of time.
The matter my hon. friend (Mr. Logan) has in mind has engaged my attention. I would not like

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The remarks that have been made with regard to superior court judges apply also to the county court judges of the province of Manitoba. Their responsibility is greater than that of the county court judges of the province of Ontario, because their jurisdiction is wider. I hope that the time has arrived when a revision of the salaries of our judiciary will be taken into serious consideration, and that they will be paid a remuneration more nearly adequate to tbeir services.

I have listened to this discussion with some interest, and I fall in with the views of those members who have spoken in regard to county court judges, and who think that $2,400 a year is a very small salary to pay to men who have the necessary ability to take that position. I think they should receive higher salaries. Take the ordinary business and professional men of this country, and I venture to say they will tell you that it is pretty hard to litvie on $2,400 a year. It has been pointed out by the hon. member for Hastings that when you take house rent into consideration and the expenses of living, there will be very little left at the end of the year to put by for a rainy day. I think the salaries of the senior judges of the county courts should be at least $3,000, that is quite little enough, and I hope that the Minister of Justice, in arranging the scale of salaries, will give the county court judges $3,000 a year. Asa layman I know what the people think about these matters. It would no doubt be very popular to go before the people and sav, see how the government has increased the salaries of the judges, although they have such an easy job of it. But we are here occupying responsible positions. and we must legislate for the best interests of the whole country. I know that it would be a popular stand, a position for demagogues to take, to say that the judges are paid high enough already. But as I say, we must legislate in the interest of justice and fair play. We must bear in mind what it costs to live: and I know very well that a judge with a family has to entertain and to keep up a social position, and to do that he requires a fair salary.
Resolution reported; read the first and second time, and agreed to.

House again in committee on Bill (No. 198) respecting Penny Banks.-The Minister of Finance.

When this Bill was in committee before, one or two clauses were reserved for the purpose of considering some suggestions that were offered in the discussion. In accordance with those suggestions I have prepared a couple of trifling amendments, not in any way affecting the general purpose of the Bill, but calculated to carry it out more effectually. In section 16, lines 17 and 18, there were some words which were thought to be obscure and it was suggested that other words might more clearly express the intention. I propose to strike out the latter part of the section and substitute other words, so that it will read as follows :
A. subscriber whose liability for his unpaid subscription shall cease and determine as hereinafter provided, shall, from the time such liability shall cease and determine, cease to bo a member of the bank.
I may remind the House that this is not an ordinary bank, but it is practically a benevolent organization, and provision is made that a certain guarantee fund should be formed. It is intended that that guarantee fund shall be a personal obligation, not following the estate of the party in the event of his death. The various parties concerned must keep the guarantee fund up to $10,000, and if any person who is concerned in that guarantee fund dies, as he ceases to be a member of the bank, his estate also ceases from all liability. But a new person must be substituted, so that at all times they will have a guarantee of $10,000. That is the purpose, which. I think, is more clearly expressed in these words than in the original words.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
On section 33,

Another section in which a change is suggested is section 33, which has reference to the statements to be presented by the bank. Tlie suggestion was offered that these statements shall be certified to by a chartered accountant. I thought that was a fair suggestion, and having considered it, I now beg to insert the following amendment:
To each of such statements shall be annexed a certificate from a chartered acountant that he has examined and audited the books of the bank and that he finds that such statement is a true statement of the affairs of the bank on the date named therein.
That is a change from the law as regards ordinary banks ?
Yes. The position of an ordinary bank would not apply to this at all. This is not a banking association for profit.
Some of these penny banks might be far removed from where a chartered accountant is to be found. Chartered accountants are only to be found in the large cities as a rule.

I think it would be necessary that they would have to retain a chartered accountant to examine the books of the bank. I thought the suggestion was a reasonable one, and I was very glad to consent to it.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if this legislation is borrowed from the English legislation upon this same subject ?
No, it is not.
Are there not any banks in England organized on a somewhat similar basis ?
There are penny banks, but I do not think they are organized on these lines at ail.
Where did the idea of this particular kind of penny bank originate ? Was it in our own country ?

It originated from a proposal made by some gentlemen in Toronto, during the last session of parliament, who desired that an organization which already exists there-in fact I think there is more than one-could he brought under some legal organization in the way of receiving a charter. We took tlie ground then that it was not wise to organize special savings banks in Canada, because the government has adopted the savings bank business as its special function, but we intimated to these gentlemen last session that we would look into. the matter and see if we could not devise a general plan whereby these penny banks might become incorporated and as well as others having a like object. They drafted a Bill which has been reviewed and changed, and the result is this Bill now before tlie committee.
Mr. DaRIVIERE. Does the hon. minister think it is wise to call this a bank ? It is not a bank, but a savings society. Is it wise to apply the name of bank to it, because we forbid any company or individual to assume tlie name of bank, or banker, or banking institution, which is not entitled to do so, and I do not see why we should apply that name to an institution of this sort.

My hon. friend (Mr. I.nRivieve) is quite right. No-

body ean use the term 'bank' except by the special authority of this parliament, but the term ' penny bank ' conveys a meaning to industrious and thrifty people which is convenient. We did not object to the title, but we were desirous that it should be surrounded by certain safeguards.

The word 'penny' qualifies the word 'bank' and gives it limited sense. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance will remember that when this matter came up before, 1 called his attention to the subject of co-operative banks, of which we have one in tlie town of Levis, and although I do not deny that an institution such as is contemplated by this Bill will do a great deal of good, particularly to people who are unfamiliar with that kind of institution to a large extent throughout this country ; I would ask the hon. minister to endeavour to obtain the opinion of some competent man in his department as to the project which I urged upon his attention previously-the establishment of co-operative banks. I conceive that these banks will do a great deal of good in the province of Quebec. They are doing a great deal of good wherever they have been established in Europe. I hold in my hand a memorandum, which X intended to quote, but which I will not, in order not to take up the time of the Committee, prepared by a well recognized authority on the subject, Mr. Wolff, who lias written a very complete work on the operation of co-operative banks. This memorandum lias been communicated to some persons in this country interested in the establishment of co-operative banks in response to an inquiry as to the working of these banks in Europe, and it refers in a special manner to the conditions existing in Canada. As a matter of fact, these co-operative banks are intended specially to facilitate tlie operations of people who could not obtain credit at tlie ordinary banks on account of tlie smallness of their means and on account of their not being accustomed to deal with banks. These banks are intended to procure credit for these people, and are particularly useful to an agricultural population. They have been established in Germany, there is a very large number of them in France, there are a great many of them in Italy and for the last two or three years, X think, they have become the subject of legislation in England. There are over one hundred and fifty of these hanks established in India at the present time. There are some in Barbadoes, and everywhere tliey have produced the most excellent results, not only in tlie way of procuring credit for people who require it. but also, as stated in this memorandum which I hold iii my band and which emanated from Mr. Wolff, by giving an education to the people in business and monetary matters and in absolutely elevating the tone of the whole community. Although it may appear strange at first sight, it is perfectly Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
true that these banks in no way interfere with the ordinary banks, that their establishment has been encouraged by the great hanks of Europe and that, as a matter of fact, they help the working of the great banks by procuring business for them which otherwise they would be precluded from taking. I think that, under these circumstances and from the fact that Mr. Wolff, having been fully informed of our circumstances hero and of the character of our agricultural resources, has expressed in this memorandum the opinion that co-operative banks would undoubtedly be a great success in Canada, that they would do a great deal of good in this country, the subject recommends itself to the attention of the hon. Minister of Finance, and I hope that before long it will so occupy the attention of the department that it will be possible for tlie bon. gentleman to give us some general legislation as to these banks which will permit of their establishment everywhere throughout the country.
Mr. BARKER, Section 33 requires that the returns shall be ' verified by the oath of the president or of one of the vice-presidents of the bank, or of the chairman of the board,' but it does not require in terms that it shall be verified by the manager. I suppose it is intended, and if so, instead of using the words ' and by the manager,' you should say ' and of the manager.'
I think the manager is included.
The statement is not verified by his oath. It is simply provided that it shall be verified by the manager. It should be made to read ' and of the manager,' so as to follow the preceding words.

That certainly is the intention, and if the intention is not carried out. T would be very glad to have it amended to read :
The oath of the president or of one of the vice-presidents of the bank, or of the chairman of the board, and of the manager or other chief officer of the bank.
It should be ' and of the manager.' It should read 'of' instead of 'by.' I am very glad to accept my hon. friend's suggestion. I move that the word ' of ' be inserted instead of ' by ' in the sixteenth line. With regard to the observations of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), I may remind him that on a previous occasion, I made the statement that my attention had been drawn to that subject by several hon. members of tlie House, and also by a gentleman on the official staff of the House of Commons, who has, I believe, connection with one of these banks which has been in operation for several years in the town of Levis.	I promised that the
matter would receive consideration, and my officials have been gathering information concerning it : not. however, I may say.

witli any expectation that we should be able to do anything with it at the present session. Owing to my very many pressing engagements, I have not been able to give it much personal attention, but I will see that during the recess the matter is further considered. So far as representations were made to me, X was led to believe that these institutions, one or two of which already exist in Canada, have been doing a very satisfactory service.
On section 29,

I want to say, Sir, just a word on that clause. There was a little misconception as to its meaning. The impression seemed to have reached the minds of some hon. gentlemen that the securities herein mentioned might be chosen for the investment of the general funds of the bank. Such, however, is not intended. The funds which may be collected from depositors cannot be invested in anything. They must be deposited in the government savings bank, and this clause has relation entirely to the small fund which is the guarantee fund, and which is the money of the promoters themselves and not the money of the depositors. They cannot invest a cent of the depositors' money in any security whatever; it must be put in the savings bank. But, we think that they should be allowed a reasonable degree of liberty, corresponding to some extent with the privilege we grant to insurance companies, respecting the investment of their own moneys, which, in this case, is only a comparatively small sum. I think when it is understood that the clause means only that, there can be no objection to it.
The "clause applies purely to the guarantee fund ?
Yes, entirely.
And the nature of the securities.
They may have some money which they want to invest, and they are free to do so in anything that is a legitimate security.

Iii one of the clauses it is provided that the incorporators cannot invest in certain funds. Where does their profit come, in the operation of the bank ? You provide that they shall receive deposits and only pay on them the same rate of interest as the government savings bank or the post office savings bank, which is a very low rate. I have no doubt that they might loan out that money at a much higher rate of interest, and thereby earn something. But, if I correctly get the sense of this legislation, it does not allow them any profit.

I can say to my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) that the
whole intention is that there shall be no profit in the transaction. It is practically a benevolent organization. There is no intention to make a profit, and if they can get out of this investment, together with the slightly increased interest the government allows them, enough to pay working expenses, that is all that is expected. It is not a profit-making organization at all.
Do you make any provision as to what their salaries shall be ?

No; the chief promoters will receive no salary whatever. They may have to employ clerical help, but it is not intended there will be any salaries to the principal promoters at all. Now, Sir, with regard to section 38, we have made provision there regarding penalties for officers of the bank who mak.e false returns, and I want to include in that penal clause the chartered accountant whose certificate is attached, so that the same penalty shall apply to the chartered accountant as will apply to any other officer who makes a false return. I move to amend this clause by inserting after the word ' bank ' in line 41 the words, ' and every chartered accountant,' and also after the word ' report,' in lines 35 and 42, the word 1 certificate.'

Amendment agreed to, and. section, as amended, agreed to.

passed.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved the second reading of Bill (No. 23S) to amend chapter 8 of the statutes of 1899, respecting the Bounties on Steel and Iron, and to provide for the payment of bounties on certain articles manufactured from steel.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into Committee thereon.

This Bill is exactly in the form of the resolutions; it contains no other provisions whatever, and the resolutions were fully considered in the Committee of the Whole.
On section 1,
Has the hon. minister made any estimate as to what he expects to have to pay per annum on these new items ?

The bounties proposed on structural iron, plates and rods, the new items covered by this Bill, are estimated roughly on about one-third of the importation of last year. Assuming that we make one-third of the importation during this year, we will pay about $150,000 for the first year. Of course, if we make more than that, the'bounty will be proportionately increased. It may increase until we replace almost the whole of our importation, which would mean a bounty of about $100,000 as respects these items.

Information has been conveyed to me that iron and steel is imported in large quantities from Canada into the United States in pig-iron and billets, and comes back to us in a manufactured condition. I understand that there is in the United States a duty of $6 a ton upon what is the raw material to those who manufacture tools of all sorts, and that having gone through the process of manufacture there, Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
that materia] comes back to us in the shape of finished tools and instruments of all kinds, on which the manufacturers get a drawback of $5.99 a ton. I am informed that there is a considerable trade of that kind. Has the minister any knowledge of that ?

I think it was the case some time ago to a limited extent, but I do not think it is the case now. The producers of steel billets in Canada, not finding a market for their product here, sent it to the United States where it was manufactured into wire rods. The manufacturers In the United States paid the duty, as my hon. friend has stated, and they would be entitled to a drawback on their exports to Canada, the wire rods coming in free. Under this Bill I do not think that will take place. Indeed, I do not think it is being done at the present time, because the producers of billets in the United States have interfered with it.

Will the importation of wire rods cease with this bounty which we are giving for the production of wire rods, does my hon. friend anticipate ? There are large quantities of wire rods imported from the United States at this moment, as well as a great deal of wire.

As soon as the Canadian manufacturers find themselves in a positon to produce these articles,
I think the importation of wire rods from the United States will largely, if not wholly, cease.

I have in my hand a letter from a gentleman who has been for a long time engaged in business, and he thinks it would have been a much better plan to have given a bounty only for pig-iron made from Canadian ore. My remembrance of the discussion that took place when it was proposed to give this bounty was to the effect that to make certain grades of iron it was necessary to import certain ores from the other side. Therefore we provided that the government give a bounty of $2 per ton on pig-iron made from foreign ore and $3 when made from native ore. This gentleman thinks that the development would have been much more rapid and greater had we confined the bounty to pig-iron made only from Canadian ore. I do no know whether the minister paid much attention to that or not. Another suggestion he makes seems to me to be very valuable. He claims that the Americans have rather disparaged our ores and refused to buy them on the ground that they contain too much sulphur, yet they are using their own ores w-hich contain a very much larger percentage of the sulphur and say they are all right. This leads him to the conclusion that they are doing this in order to depreciate our mineral properties and purchase them at lower prices ? He thinks that the government I have it in their hands to help the Canadian

mine-owners and the development of Canadian mines to a much greater extent, if the suggestions he made were carried out.

The suggestion that the bounty should be confined entirely to iron made from Canadian ore is so natural that it has been frequently made, and was fully considered some years ago. The provision giving a portion of the bounty to pig-iron made from foreign ore was inserted at the instance of the manufacturers themselves. They consider it desirable to have ores from different sources so as to blend them together, and thereby make a more perfect article than can be produced from the one ore. That system of blending different ores is adopted by iron men generally. The whole question was well considered, and it was not thought wise to refuse the bounty in the case of foreign ore, but a distinction is made. A bounty of 83 is given to iron made from Canadian ore, and $2 to iron made from imported ore. To have confined the bounty entirely to iron made from native ore would, in the opinion of the trade, have proved embarrassing to the iron industry. Newfoundland ore is counted as imported ore.

When at Sault Ste. Marie, l was told that it was absolutely necessary to mix the ore from Michipicoten with ore purchased from the United States in order to produce good material. We are coming to the assistance mainly of one company in passing this Bill, and I think it is a pity we did not go over the whole iron industry and adopt a general system of protection, which would cover every article manufactured from iron and steel as against the United States. This is confined to wire rods, rolled angles and rolled plates, but we would find a great deal more to be protected if we were to go over the whole list. Our importations from the United States of iron and articles manufactured from iron are increasing at a very considerable rate. Last year we imported in agricultural implements over 81,000,000 worth, pig-iron over $600,000; electrical apparatus, $1,500,000; hardware over $600,000; machinery, over $3,000,000; scales, over $100,000 ; tools and machines of all kinds, nearly $600,000. If we look at the latest reports of the United States, covering the eight months ending February, 1901,	1902 and 1903,
we will find that the increase in importations from the United States in these lines of manufactured goods were very considerable indeed. Take for instance, electric appliances, in February, 1902, we imported $17,000 worth, in February, 1S93, $47,000, and for the eight months ending February, 1892, $442,000 worth, and the eight months ending February. 1903. $516,000 Worth. For the same period, 1902, we imported $604,000 worth of hardware, tools and sawis and the following year, $1,158,000 worth. If we go over the different exports
from the United States to British North America, of productions resulting from the manufacture of iron, we find that the importations are increasing enormously every year, although I have no doubt that this system of bounties should have a beneficial effect, particularly with regard to the industries mentioned in the discussion to-day. But I think it is a pity that, with the immense mineral resources at our hand, we should not be able to exclude completely American productions, and keep the commerce entirely for our own market. I believe that we should move in that direction.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

maintopic: STEAMSHIP SERVICE BETWEEN CANADA AND FRANCE.

speechtext:
House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
Resolved, that it is expedient to make provision for a subsidy, not exceeding $133,333.33 a year, for a steamship service between Canada and France.-The Minister of Trade and Commerce.

maintopic: STEAMSHIP SERVICE BETWEEN CANADA AND FRANCE.
speechtext: I do not intend to pass this resolution through Committee, as I have not all the information I want to place in the hands of the House. The government have passed a contract with Mr. Colombier, of Bordeaux. He is a ship owner of some importance. We have a contract, which I shall lay upon the Table of the House, not at this sitting, but at the next sitting ; but I will give the substance of it now. The contract stipulates for a line of steamers to ply between Canada and Bordeaux, and ports of France, eighteen trips during the year-twelve trips during the ' summer months and six trips during the winter months. I may say that I have not the honour of knowing Mr. Colombier personally. He applied to tlie government, bringing letters of inti'oductlon from leading bankers of Bordeaux, establishing the fact that he was a member of a firm of some magnitude. But, not satisfied with that, I Cabled to the British consul of Bordeaux. I will bring down the answer we received from that gentleman. It was to the effect that the House of Colombier was a very respectable bouse, that it could not be said to be one of very large financial means, though respectable ; find that he understood that, for such an undertaking as this, Mr. Colombier had the capital necessary. With this assurance, we thought we could deal with Mr. Colombier. Tlie advantage of a line of steamers between Canada and France has been long recognized on both sides of the House. A statute was passed in the first session of 1896-the last session of the late government-providing for a subsidy of $50,000 for a line of communication between France 1 and Canada. This subsidy was found to
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

maintopic: STEAMSHIP SERVICE BETWEEN CANADA AND FRANCE.
speechtext:
There is no doubt whatever that it is extremely desirable for us to extend our trade relations with France. Anybody who takes the trouble to consult the statistics relating to the trade between Canada and France, and who knows anything of the possibilities of commerce with that great country, must promptly come to the conclusion that we are yearly losing a very large trade with France. When my right lion, friend (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was in France on the occasion of his last visit we had an intimation that he was negotiating for the extension of our treaty rights with France. In the same way, we had frequent intimations that the Alinister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) was endeavouring to negotiate with the gentlemen who, at one time, represented Italy in this country, the basis of a treaty of,commerce with that country which would have been extremely profitable to us. If I mistake not, neither of these endeavours came to anything. The efforts made by the then Italian consul in the city of Alontreal were so barren of results that he gave up the attempt to arrive at any agreement with this government, and, if I am not mistaken, resigned his position.
But to come back to France. I think if it is desirable that we should establish better commercial relations with that country experience has taught us that we must proceed with great care, and that we should
10800

take every precaution to see that the efforts which we have made in the past in regard to the establishment of a line of steamers between Canada and France, and which have failed in a discouraging manner, should not fail upon this occasion. It is, as I have already suggested, very difficult to calculate to what extent our trade with France would increase if it could be put upon a proper basis, and particularly in view of the special commercial and tariff regulations of France, if we could establish a line which would be of a permanent character, and offer a permanent guarantee of success. I have taken the trouble to look up, in the last statistical year-book of Canada, some figures of our trade with France in the past. It has not been nearly as considerable as it might be. My right hon. friend has mentioned the article of pulp. There is no doubt that if we had a line of steamers 'doing a direct business with France we would have a very large market for our pulp ; although I have always clung to the idea that we should, as much as possible, keep our pulp here and manufacture it into paper ourselves. Still, there is no doubt that, with the immense quantity of pulp wood we have at our disposal some pulp must be exported, and there is an immense field in France for selling pulp if we could only establish that trade. A few days ago, in travelling up from Quebec, I met a very wealthy capitalist who had just come out from France, and who is interested in large cement works in that country. He was coming out here to see what opportunities there were for carrying on a cement business in this country, and I have no doubt that if facilities presented themselves for a trade in cement, a very large trade in that particular article could be developed with old France. Now let me give a few figures to the House showing wliat our expox-ts have been to France, taking up first the article of mineral products :
