I think there is no doubt that the nickle, of which we possess almost the exclusive production, with the exception of one other country, I believe, we could do a very extensive trade with France and with Italy. I was credibly informed the other day that a very large industrial company in France had sent out an agent here prepared to purchase any quantity of nickle matte. There are several other industrial companies in France besides this one who have carried the manufacture of the by-products from nickle to a greater degree of perfection than the manufacturers of any other country, and these companies would be rivals of the present American purchasers of that metal. But, as I said a moment ago, we have failed up to the present moment to establish a proper line of steamers witli France, and I believe that in many respects we have failed to cultivate our trade relations with that country as we should, because with France, Belgium, Italy and other countries of Europe we could do a far greater exporting trade than we are doing now. Every effort we can make in that direction should be made. We have in France, as representative, a gentleman who is well known to many of the members of this House, and than whom we could find no better representative. Mr. Fabre represents the Canadian interests in France with great success, and fills the place assigned him with a great perfection. Nevertheless he has now reached a certain age, he is a lawyer, and he has not been trained to commercial customs and habits of business. I think it would be well for. us to have in France, as we have in other countries, a purely commercial agent. We should have in France a person under Mr. Fabre's control, who would pay exclusive attention to the commercial relations of this country with France. My right hon. friend may say that we have at present there a commercial representative. There is a gentleman by the name of Mr. Poindron, who has been appointed by the government as commercial representative in France. Mr

Poindron is a very estimable gentleman, I am acquainted with, him, but he has not always lived in this country, he is not a Canadian, and I question very much it he is the most competent man we could find to till that position, and to carry out the objects I have just mentioned. I think we would require under Mr. Fabre's control a gentleman whose time should be taken up with commercial matters, a gentleman well acquainted with the conditions of the trade of this country, fully 'au fait ' with all our resources, who would from time to time report to this government, and who would display a greater activity than I think it is possible for Mr. Poindron to do, who is not of Canadian origin, who is not as fully conversant with the commercial situation of this country as would be a man selected with that qualification in view. As regards this steamship line, as my right hon. friend knows, we have failed in that twice already, and it is important for us to be fully informed before we go into a third venture. These are points, for instance, upon which I would like information, and upon which I am sure other members of the committee would also desire to be fully informed: What is the cost per trip of these vessels sailing to France ? What kind of vessels shall we have ? That, I think is all important. What is the capacity of these vessels ? What is their availability for carrying freight, and I may say also for carrying passengers, because it is important that we should have a proper passenger service connected with the freight service of this line ? What is this company ? My right hon. friend has mentioned the name of Mr. Colombier,. about whom I have heard that he is a man of some means-a merchant, I believe. Is he a shipper ?

maintopic: STEAMSHIP SERVICE BETWEEN CANADA AND FRANCE.
speechtext: Yes, a shipper.

maintopic: STEAMSHIP SERVICE BETWEEN CANADA AND FRANCE.
speechtext:
Does he propose to form a company, or has he a company already formed and everything at hand necessary to carry out this service properly, or does he merely intend-as I am afraid other parties connected with the steamship line that we have subsidized in the past have done-to form a company after obtaining this subsidy? What is the nature of this company, or is it the fact that Mr. Colombier is an amateur simply, or has he a company at his command, and if there is a company actually formed, what is the capacity of the company to secure trade ? Even if we havie an agent of great activity to endeavour to open up avenues of trade, we want to deal with a responsible company having everything necessary at its command, such as other steamship lines have to secure trade. Mr. Colombier is associated in this matter, as far as I am informed, with Mr. Carbon-neau. Mr. Carbonneau, as far as I know, has been speculating in mines in the Klondike, and he has been endeavouring to sell Mr. MONK.	.
a mine there called the Gold Run to capitalists in France. He has been in Paris with that object in view, as we are well aware from the papers which have been sent out here from France, and no doubt during his stay there, in his efforts to dispose of this mine and to put through other financial ventures, he has endeavoured to start this line of steamers. I do not wish to reflect in any way upon Mr. Carbonneau, because I do not know myself anything unfavourable to him except that in the city of Montreal he was connected with a company which contributed to a large degree to the ruin of La Banque du Peuple. The connection of that company with La Banque du Peuple, from the closing of which so many people suffered in the city of Montreal, was not of a favourable nature. I believe it was the Shipping and Trading Company, of which, if I mistake not, Mr. Carbonneau was the manager. I would not, speaking perfectly frankly for myself, place very much confidence in Mr. Carbonneau, from what I know of him, for the purpose of this great undertaking, because it is a great undertaking, requiring a serious and competent man to bring it to a successful issue. I would not like the committee to think that I am considering this question in a harsh manner, because I will quote from the opinion expressed by ' Le Moniteur du Commerce.' of Montreal, a financial paper having a large circulation, a serious paper, upon this very project. This is what the ' Moniteur du Commerce ' says, and as it is in French, I will translate it into English, so that the committee may see the view that this commercial newspaper takes of this project:
The New French Line.
The daily newspaper asserts that the federal government has signed a contract for a subsidy for a direct steamship service between Canada and France, the port of Bordeaux being the terminus of this line on the other side of the Atlantic. We have had so many disappointments on the subject of projects for direct communication with ancient France that we may be permitted to be a little sceptical on the subject with the information which has been conveyed to us. Preceding projects reached only the initial stage of execution. They were not serious projects and they turned out miserable failures because the promoters seemed to be aiming rather at the obtaining of an official subsidy of a few hundred dollars than the best means of increasing our trade between France and Canada. This time once more the indications of the project are vague and insufficient to reassure commercial people. It would be regrettable that the Canadian government should have concluded to grant an annual subsidy of $100,000 or thereabouts to an organization which would not be able to offer sufficient guarantees for the proper execution of the work. It has been mentioned that the contractors with our government are such people as Mr. Colombier and Mr. Carbonneau. Very good. To what association do they belong ? What guarantees do they offer that the millions of dollars contributed and given out of the treasury of the Can-

aciian people will be employed advantageously tor the promotion of Franco-Canadian commerce which at the present moment is diminishing instead of increasing.
That is borne out by the statistics which I have quoted :
The federal department of commerce as well as the Department of Marine could perhaps inform parliament of the nature of the alleged contract which has been entered into for the establishment - of a French freight line of steamers between Bordeaux and Quebec and Montreal or any other place.
That the right hon. gentleman has promised to do.
The federal parliament will ask : Who is Mr. Colombier ? Who is Mr. Carbonneau ? Is the latter the promoter of the Shipping and Trading Company of whVh we have such an interesting recollection ? The contract in question is far too important to be allowed to pass without some comment.
That appeared on the 4th September. Tbe right bon. gentleman has stated that this contract would give us 18 trips a year. I think we should be fully informed as to tlie passenger accommodation which would be given on these steamers. I think that is more important than one would think at first sight, although, of course, the interchange of trade is the prime object. I will wait until the information which the few remarks I have just made justly call for will have been given to the committee as to the nature of the contract and the nature of the facilities afforded for carrying out this service. We are given to understand that a large amount of money is to be expended and expended, in my opinion, most usefully, because X think I can make it a reproach to this government that have not realized sufficiently our possibilities of trade with European countries, and with France particularly.
My right hon. friend remembers that 1 took some interest in tbe efforts made by tbe Italian consul at one time, to bring to a satisfactory conclusion our negotiations with regard to trade with Italy. I think we could do a very large business with those countries. In fact, if our exports of agricultural products had not increased so enormously within the past few years-from $25,000,000 in 1878 to $107,000,000 last year our trade with these countries would be practically at a standstill. This is a very good means to develop our trade with France, where, as we are all aware, the regulations are so stringent in reference to direct exportations to that country that it is impossible indirectly to establish a trade with France. However, we should surround this large grant with every precaution, and I hope the matter will be fully gone into so that we shall not fail now, as we have failed on previous occasions.

My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) stated the reason why the trade
between Canada and continental European nations has not developed as it should. It is because all nations of continental Europe, so far as I am aware, have the same tariff that France has; a double tariff favouring direct importation into their own country.
I do not think there is such a provision in the Italian tariff. I am almost certain that my right hon. friend is wrong as to Italy with regard to direct importations.

Perhaps so. Let us confine ourselves to France for the present. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) says we cannot hope to develop any trade with France unless we have a direct line of steamers. This has been the bar to all the efforts we have made up to the present. My hon. friend has alluded to the negotiations we had in France last year with a view of improving our trade. These negotiations were purely informal. I had the benefit of the assistance of the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Finance on that occasion, and I think we all agreed that it was possible to improve our trade, so as to make it very acceptable to France and to ourselves. But all these efforts are useless until and unless we have a direct line of communication with France. We could not in the past be very particular as to the establishment of that line because the offers for it have been few and far between. This is really only the second offer we have received since we came into office in 1890. Mr. Colombier is a shipper of some importance in Bordeaux. As to that I have got direct information from Bordeaux itself. Beyond doubt his house is one of great respectability. Tbe contract that we have is with Mr. Colombier himself, and no one else. We have no contract whatever with Mr. Carbonneau whom we do not know officially. The only contract we have is with the house of Colombier. Naturally, Mr. Colombier expects to form a company; hut there is a provision in the contract that it cannot be assigned, except with the consent of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, so that if Mr. Colombier is not himself able to perform the service he has undertaken; if he wants the assistance of some other capitalists to join with him in that most laudable1 object; he must come to the government and we have to judge of the character, and the stability of the company which is to perform the service before we are called on to agree to it. This is one of tbe express provisions of the contract. As to the character of the service which is to he given, the contract itself will give to my hon. friend ail the information which he desires.
When may we expect to have this contract ?

We should have had it to-day. if I thought the matter would be reached, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce lias charge of tlie matter,
10S11

and it was too late to get it when I knew the question was to come up. 1 do not propose to take this matter out of Committee to-day, and at the next sitting we shall have all the papers brought down for the information of the House. My hon. friend shall find in the contract information as to the number of ships-if I remember right it is four, as to their capacity which I think is about 4,000 tons, and as to their accommodation for passengers and freight.
Does Mr. Colombier own any ships ?

Mr. Colombier is a ship owner, and does a large business in the Mediterranean. As to that, I have the most positive assurance. Mr. Colombier proposes to have new ships built especially for this trade, with accommodation for passengers. and not only for ordinary freight but for express freight, and also refrigerators. He proposes in a word, that the ships should l>e, as the contract provides, of the most modern pattern. It is useless for me to dilate upon these points, because all this information will be found in the contract itself.
At six o'clock. Committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at Eight o'clock.

When you left the Chair at six o'clock, I was about to make an inquiry of the Premier. I understood him to say that he liacj data which warranted him in believing that we could do a valuable trade with France in certain lines. Would he be kind enough to lay that data on the Table, so that it may be available to all of us ? Would he also let us know whether he has made any inquiry as to the specific lines of trade ? He mentioned two articles, agricultural implements and cement, in which he thought we might profitably increase our trade. There may be other lines on which I assume the information he has would be interesting and valuable to the House ; and we should consider these points before determining whether or not we should support the resolution. I believe some business is done with France at the present time in agricultural implements. I happen to have a nephew in France at present, establishing an agency for one of the agricultural firms, and he writes to me that he thinks there will be a very valuable trade done in the future. At present their business in France is carried on through London. It may be that the favourable duty clause could be taken advantage of if we had a direct connection with France, which cannot be done now. He mentioned also that there was a great demand for cement, in which a good business could be done, provided that it could be laid down at a certain figure. He also Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
mentioned pulp, which, however, he said was more uncertain. He mentioned several other lines in which he thought a profitable trade could be done. I think we should make a strong effort to establish and develop trade with that great country, because, from several letters which I have received from him, it seems to me to offer great possibilities ; and he has spent the most of the last three years there. As to whether we can make a trade with France pay, the history of the past gives us very little encouragement. Whether the difficulties have been such as can be overcome from this side is a question which I presume none of us can answer ; but I presume that the Premier has endeavoured to ascertain what the obstacles have been, and whether they can be overcome by a direct line of steamships. It seems to me that we ought to know what facilities there will be for carrying various lines of produce. Possibly a trade might be established in some of the dairy lines. In that event cold storage accommodation would be required if we hoped to develop it as we should. The passenger trade as well is a matter of importance. I think the Premier said that this company were expected to make about eighteen trips in a year. Whether that will be enough or not I do not know. I presume it would at least be a fair test of what could be done. We are told that we have a valuable agent there, Mr. Fabre. I do not: know why the right hon. gentleman should come to that conclusion, for while I believe that Mr. Fabre is a very estimable gentleman individually, I do not know that he has ever done anything to develop our trade with France. He went there first as an immigration agent. I remember looking up the record some time ago, when I found that lie had sent out three immigrants in the course of the year. Our trade with France does not seem to be developing as we might reasonably expect it to do, if we had a live, active, commercial agent there, I think a great deal more could be accomplished. In one of his communications to me, my nephew said he thought we should have an active agent there. I drew his attention to the fact that Mr. Fabre was there ; but he replied that so far as he knew, Mr. Fabre was not known in commercial life at all. He thought it would be a matter of importance to have an active commercial agent, who would advertise the country and endeavour to put people in France handling lines that we could furnish in communication with those producing them here. He thinks an important trade could be done in the agricultural implement line. The firm he represents are establishing agencies in France, and I think they intend to follow up their work there by establishing another in Russia, where he also thinks a valuable trade could be done. We are voting a considerable sum of money for this steamship line, and I think we

ought to know something about the firm taking it up. 1 was about to ask the Premier if he would not think it worth while to advertise for tenders, to see if he could not have other offers as well as the one he lias. 1 presume he has not yet closed with this company. Then, we should be informed as to the financial strength of the company, and as to its commercial relations with the people of France. It ought to be a company engaged in shipping, either as owner or agent ; it ought to be financially strong ; and it ought to be prepared to further the efforts of those endeavouring to establish lines of commerce with France. I would suggest that we ought to have a live agent appointed there, because, with all respect to Mr. Fabre, 1 do not think that lie is in touch with the commercial life in France.

I have listened with special interest to the remarks of the hon. member for East Grey in regard to the importance of appointing a live commercial agent in Paris. I was in Paris for some time, about a year ago, and while everybody seemed to have the highest opinion of Mr. Fabre as a very estimable gentleman, 1 found an almost unanimous opinion that he was not in touch with the commerce of France ; and if we are going- to spend a large sum of money to subsidize a steamship line between Canada and France, we certainly should have a good commercial agent in that country. The trade between this country and the French republic should be a very large one, for many reasons, and if we are going to pay this large subsidy, which 1 think is an excellent thing to do, we should have at the other end of the line a good commercial agent of Canada, who would make himself known, not only in Paris but in the north and south of France.

As a representative of the city of Montreal, I have had something to do with this matter, not only in the present instance, but on former occasions when attempts were made to establish a line of steamers between France and Montreal. Up to the present, four efforts were made, the first of them dating as far back as ten years ago, and they were all failures. On this occasion the government is taking every precaution to achieve success. There can be no doubt that better communication is needed between France and Canada, particularly in the interests of trade. If you will look, Sir, to the figures in the report of the Minister of Trade and Commerce for the last year, you will be surprised at the facts you will find there. I take from the blue-book of the year ending the 30th of June, 1902, the following figures, and I have taken only the chief articles of French import. A most extraordinary fact is that while France imports from foreign countries $113,000,000 of goods, out of that only $309,920 worth come from Canada. Take
for instance, the item of live stock, there was imported into France from the 30th of June, 1901 to the 30th of June, 1902 $10,200,000 worth.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Where from ?

I have not all the details, but of that amount only $129,000 worth came from Canada, and according to the best possible authority at least $2,000,000 worth might be taken from Canada if the proper facilities were furnished. In butter, $4,000,000 worth were imported into France from foreign countries, and not a cent's worth from Canada. '
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Have you any idea how much butter was exported from France ?

No, but the possibilities are that $2,000,000 worth of butter might be exported from Canada to France, if proper means were taken. Cheese, over $7,000,000 worth were imported by France from foreign countries, aud not a cent's worth from Canada. In that line there is a possibility of our sending to France a million dollar's worth. Green fruits, such as apples, and canned fruits, $5,000,000 worth were imported by France, and but $1,700 worth from Canada. The possibilities there are that we might count with certainty on sending $1,200,000 worth to France. Wheat, corn and flour, $8,000,000 worth were imported by France from foreign countries, and only $175,000 worth from Canada. Those who are competent to judge say that we could increase that trade to $3,500,000 if we went the right way about it. Raw hides were imported by France from foreign countries to the extent of $27,000,000 worth, and only $2,320 worth from Canada. In that line also we could make a large increase, amounting to some $2,000,000. Meats, $5,100,000 imported into France from foreign countries and none whatever from Canada, yet there is a possibility of sending $1,500,000 worth to France. Lard and tallow $4,000,000 worth imported from foreign countries and none from Canada. Those in a position to judge say we could sell a million dollars worth of lard. Deals and other lumber, $35,000,000 were imported by France of which only $200,000 worth came from Canada. In that line there is certainly great possibility, according to people who know, of our increasing 'Mir exports to $10,000,000. Staves, $7.000,000 were imported into Bordeaux, which is the chief place of consumption, and none from Canada. There is a total of $113,960, 000 foreign goods imported by France, of which only $391,921 worth came from Canada, and there is a possibility of that export being increased to $25,000,000. To show that one of the gentlemen connected with this new undertaking seems to have studied the question and to understand the situation

is the fact that Mr. Colombier went through Ontario and made a special study of the question of staves. After having discovered from the blue-book what had been Imported into France from foreign countries, he affirms, under his signature, that these $7,000,000 worth could be imported from Canada. Another article that did not appear in the statement I have just read to the House, is the item of pulp wood. At present France gets all its supply from Sweden and Norway, but no doubt a considerable portion would be taken from this country. Another article which has not been mentioned but concerning which inquiry was made by Mr. Colombier, is the article of railway ties.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Is there a firm ?

Yes, Colombier Bros., of Bordeaux, a very old firm, connected with transportation. They have been in the trade for the last twenty-five or thirty years, and therefore have been in the habit of studying all the different kinds of imports and exports. Mr. Colombier is confident that we could export to France over 400,000 ties per year. There was a contract offered to him for ten years at the rate of 400,000 railway ties a year. Of course, it is such a big contract that it was very difficult to say whether it could be undertaken. I mention these facts only to show the advantages that could be got from the establishment of such a line. I should think that every body would agree to the proposition. The offer made the government was one which does not entail any serious engagement as regards money.
If these people are not ready to carry out the contract which they offered to carry out, of course no money will be disbursed by the government. But it will show once more how ready the government of Canada is to do anything in its power to establish new channels for trade. France has a population of 37,000.000 and. from the figures I have given it must strike every one that this trade has been neglected up to the present time. I do not blame the different governments; it has probably been due to circumstances and to difficulties that have not been foreseen. But when people who understand the transportation question take up this enterprise, people who will be able to establish, not only in Bordeaux but all over France, agencies for the gathering of trade for Canada, and who will also establish proper agencies in this country for return cargoes. I have no doubt that'they can make this business very profitable. There is an example in Montreal at the present time. The Robert Reford Company have been doing quite an extensive trade in Mediterranean ports, bringing fruits to Canada. They have made quite a success of it by confining themselves almost entirely to one line of goods. There is no reason ill Hon. Mr. PREFONTAINE.
the world why a company properly organized, with people who know their business and undertake with the idea of making it a success, should not be able to carry on work of great advantage to Canada and to increase wonderfully our export trade. Of course, the difficulty with the French line is very easy to understand. It is not so much the return cargo, for, with good agents, I think a line to France could always find a return cargo, but it is to find a cargo from France here. Colombier Bi-others seem to understand that perfectly well. They are up-to-date, and seem to know exactly what is wanted. They have lines to South America, and also lines out of Vancouver. They know the ground on which they are working. This is an occasion when the government may fairly claim credit for having done its duty to the country.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Speaking of the trade in cement, do I undei'stand that we are to import it, or do we send it to France ?

France was to take it from U3, That is What Mr. Lefebvre told me. There is no doubt that we can develop a very large trade. But we shall require full Information as to the details of the contract. If it is satisfactory. I for one, would 339
be greatly in favour of establishing this line.

As I stated a few hours ago, the contract will be laid on the Table of the House. That will be the best way to give my hon. friends on the other side the information they desix-e. With regard to the party with whom we are contracting, Mr. Colombier, the government are not able to give more information than that we have received from the consul at Bordeaux. It appears from that information that he is a ship-owner of great respectability, and although not standing in the very front rank of the business, he is able to take hold of the subsidy which the government of Canada is anxious to give to some one. We have been disappointed more thaxr once, and have applied in diffex'ent quarters without any results. When I was in Great Britain last year, I had sevex-al interviews with Sir Alfred Jones, of the Elder-Dempster Line, and I almost succeeded in inducing him to take clxax-ge of this service and to take the subsidy which we are to provide for it. I have reason to believe that Sir' Alfred .Tones would have accepted the service were it not that he had disposed of the largest part of his ships to the Canadian Pacific Railway, and they were not available for that service. Now, with regard to the agency we have in France, not only Mr. Fabre, who is more of a diplomatic than a commercial agent, but we have appointed Mr. Poindron, who is a very excellent gentleman, and whom I consider more valuable than my hon. friend from Jacques Car-tier is inclined to consider him. He is familiar not only with France, but witlx Canada. He resided for two or thx-ee yeax-s in Canada when he was agent of the" line which had but a sliox-t duration, and in which Mr. Clergue, of Sauit Ste. Marie, held the largest interest. He has also been agent for a .Canadian line for some time plying to tbe port of Bordeaxxx. He has, therefore, acquired a pretty accux-ate knowledge of the condition of trade in this country: he also knows the tx-ade of France perfectly well, and when we have this line in operation we will be able to see what he can do. at all events. Mr. Poindron is there really on trial. His report will be brought down. If he succeeds, well and good; if lie does not, of course the government will have to look for somebody else.

How long has he been there ?
The PRIME MINISTER, Since the month of September a year ago.

I had some correspondence with this young man who was there, and he had no knowledge of him, and I directed him to hunt up Mr. Fabre. His answer was that Mr. Fabre could not be regarded as a commercial agent, but was rather the representative of the country.



TUe PRIME MINISTER. Mr. Poindron is the commercial agent whose business it is to look after trade matters alone. When I said a moment ago that we had ample data to justify our expectation of developing a large trade, I did not mean to say that we had any particular data. But\we have the report of Mr. Poindron, and I venture to say that the public data we have justifies all the expectations which have been entertained on both sides of the House.
I did not understand what the minister meant by direct trade. "Would it not be equally a direct trade if the steamships were to call at other ports?

No, the moment the steamship leaves Canada and goes to Southampton and crosses to France, all the goods are subjected to a surtax on the boat. Therefore, in order to have fair-play under the treaty, we must have a direct line from port to port.

I think the French government, in a case of this character, a direct line going straight from Canada to France, gives a bounty in some shape, so many francs per ton of the vessel. Perhaps the Minister of Marine and Fisheries could inform me.

I do not remember the exact sum which is given by the French government per ton to every vessel, whether it is in a line between France and Canada or France and any other country. There is a general law, and all proprietors of ships have the privilege of taking advantage of that law. But the vessels must be under French register. In this ease, it could only apply to two of the ships, because two have got to fly the British flag. So what they would gain on one side by sailing under French register, they will lose on the two which will sail the British flag.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Then, there would be four ships?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Are these ships in existence to-day ?
I understand they are under contract to be built, to be delivered on the 1st of April next.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Has this question been referred either to Mr. Fabre or to Mr. Poindron, or did these gentlemen, Mr. Car-bonneau and Mr. Colombier, bring letters from either of our agents in France ?
We had nothing to do with Mr. Carbonneau, but only with Mr. Colombier. We cabled to Bordeaux to
ascertain the standing of these gentlemen, and I will bring dowrn the telegram.
Why did you not apply to your agent in France for that purpose ?
Mr. Fabre is located in Paris, and we thought it advisable to get information of the sanding of Mi-. Colombier direct from the consul at Bordeaux.
What is the salary paid to Mr. Poindron ? Has he made any report, and has it been brought down ?
I understand he has made more than one report, but it has not been brought down. I could not say at the moment what his salary is.

I would like to get some information from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries on another question. We had before the House a short time ago the question of subsidizing vessels to take Canadian products to South Africa. I was not quite clear then as to the conditions under which this service was to be performed. We find, however, that vessels subsidized to go to South Africa were permitted to take the produce of the United States, which entered! into competition with our own produce in South African markets; that these vessels received part of their cargo from the United States, and that while the Canadian people had to bear the burden of the subsidy, the American exporters derived part of the advantage. We find also in the case of the steamers plying on the Pacific, that while they are subsidized and have been assisted by the people of Canada, they also carry American manufactures to Japan, and when our Canadian manufactures reach Japan they are subjected to a higher rate of duty than the American manufactures. I would like to know more about the subsidy to be given to the vessels which are to run direct to French ports. I have no objections at all to subsidizing a line of steamers if it will help to develop our trade and justify the expenditure. But I want to know if there are any stipulations made with regard to freight rates, with regard to the trade that we desire to promote, and if there is any provision made for rates ? I have no doubt that American exporters will take advantage of vessels running direct from Montreal or Quebec in the summer, and from Halifax and. St. John in the winter, and use them to send their goods, those in which they desire to promote trade, to France to compete with our own goods. Is there any provision made for discriminating in freight rates against American products ? The hon. gentleman will see that if the Canadian people are to pay for chartering these vessels, for subsidizing lines to run to Japan, to run to South Africa and to run to France, it would be unfair- that our American friends, who are competitors with us in

many of those articles we export, should be permitted to come in and take advantage of these subsidized lines. I think they should, if they are getting the use of these vessels, pay a portion of the subsidy ; and it seems to me that if some reasonable provision of that kind is not made it will be most unfair to tax the Canadian people to pay this subsidy and to allow our American competitors to get the advantage of the service without contributing anything towards it.

All I can say to my hon. friend in regard to this matter is that we had some complaints some time ago. I myself received some complaints a short time ago that the line of steamers whicli we have subsidized between Canada and South Africa was carrying American goods. I referred the matter to the Department of Trade and Commerce which replied at once to the parties who had the contract, the Allan, the Elder Dempster and the Furness line, to get an explanation on the subject. I do not know what the answer has been, but of course I can assure my hon. friend that we did not subsidize this South African line to carry American goods.

The matter came up when the subsidy for the South African line was under consideration, and the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) admitted that these vessels carried American goods. We surely cannot afford to subsidize these vessels in order that American exporters can compete with ourselves in South Africa ?
I think the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce said that he would inquire into the matter.

No, he said that it would be an advantage to our shippers because if these vessels got a full cargo they would be able to take our goods at lower rates than if the vessels were not filled. We should get some information in regard to the matter ; because, while we desire to extend our trade, we should see to it that our American competitors are not permitted to use these vessels on more favourable terms than ourselves, or even on equal terms, unless they are willing to pay a portion of the subsidy.

Mr. Chairman, I do not rise for the purpose of objecting to tins subsidy or any subsidy that will increase our trade with other countries. As I understand it this is a contract for eighteen trips and there will be no regular date of sailing.
Yes.

There will be ? Of course they will be advertised ahead, but, if we had regular weekly or fortnightly trips it would help to increase the trade.
I would like to know if anything has been 339J
done with regard to making arrangements with the Canadian Pacific Railway or any other line of steamships. The right hon. Prime Minister has stated that this must be a direct line, otherwise we cannot get the benefits that would result from a trade with France, and that if the steamer were to call at Southampton the surtax wouldl be applied. Would it not be possible to arrange with the Canadian Pacific Railway, or with any other line of steamers, for a fortnightly service, the steamer to leave Canada, go direct to France, then go to Southampton and then on their return leave Southampton, go to France and come direct to Canada ? In that way I cannot see that there would be any danger of the surtax being applied. A company like the Canadian Pacific Railway, or any other company having so many steamers, would be able to give us a fortnightly service. As I understand it there will be eighteen trips. That means $7,500 per trip or about $250 per day for each steamer even if it does not do any trade of any kind. I believe that one of these steamers can be run for almost $250 per day anid I believe it would almost pay any steamship that had as many vessels as the Canadian Pacific Railway, Allan or Dominion Line to start a steamship from Southampton, go over to France, get whatever passengers and freight are there and bring them back to Canada. Even though we had to pay $7,500 per trip for a fortnightly service, if it were well advertised I think it would be more likely to increase trade between France and Canada than to have a service for which we have to advertise a week or two ahead the day the steamer would sail. If it were understood throughout the Dominion that on a certain day you could always depend on a steamer sailing for France and at the same time for England I think it would add greatly to the usefulness of this service. I certainly would not hesitate to increase this subsidy to secure a regular fortnightly service and I think it could be got much cheaper by arranging with one of these large steamship lines to have their steamers run in the way I have indicated ; that is to leave Canada, go to France, then come over to Southampton, then return from Southampton to France, and then back to Canada. Perhaps the right hon. gentleman would say whether that could be arranged and if that would not overcome the difficulty that there may be in the way of the service.
The only thing I know is that this subsidy has been going begging for several years and that all these large companies have been unwilling to tackle it.
Have these companies been offered an amount equal to $7,500 a trip ?
We have been approached by nobody except this firm.
$133,000 for eighteen trips. Has it been put in that way to these companies ?

$133,000 is to be paid in case they make twenty-four trips. It is provided that they shall make eighteen trips and get $100,000 which is equal to $5,000 per trip. This resolution provides for $133,000 and the contract specifies that they need only make eighteen trips.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Raymond Prefontaine).

speechtext: The contract is for eighteen trips for which they will receive $100,000, but they can increase the number up to twenty-four trips and receive $133,000.

I would like to ask the right hon. gentleman If any precautions have been taken to protect Canadian exporters against discrimination in rates ? Suppose wre contribute this $133,000 towards the establishment of this line, and find that we at once develop trade in certain articles that have been mentioned here, and then find that our American competitors in these articles can get lower rates for the carriage of their goods on these steamships than are given to Canadians, surely that wTill not be right ?
I do not know that the contract provides against it. I have not the contract here. We will have to wait until the contract comes down.
Is it not reasonable that we should have some protection of that kind ? We should not pay a subsidy in order that our American competitors may reap the advantage.
I have not the contract under my hand but it is provided in the contract that the rates are under the supervision of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I understand that this resolution will not leave the Committee tonight. I suppose we will have the contract down before we can proceed further ?
Yes.

I would like to ask my right hon. friend when he brings the contract down to be good' enough also to bring the commercial reports sent by Mr. Poindron so that we may have all the information before us.
Yes.

I think if the government would give $5,000 per trip for a fortnightly service and have the steamers run direct from this country to France and then to Southampton it would be an advantage.
Sir WILFRID LAL'RIER.
I think we had better start in a quiet and modest manner before undertaking that.
I have discovered in my notes that it is provided in the contract that there shall be no discrimination against Canadian goods and that Canadian merchants shall always have the preference.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I am glad to know that there is to be no discrimination. I think they should have an advantage in respect to freight rates.
It is in the contract that Canadian merchants have the preference in the shipment of their goods and there shall be no discrimination against them.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: If they have enough Canadian products to fill the vessel, they will get the preference, but they will get no advantage as to rates. If we have a diplomatic agent in France who has been there for many years, would it not be a very good thing to cable him to ask as to the status of both these gentlemen whose names have been mentioned ? His long experience in Paris, his intimate knowledge of Canadian affairs and his intimate knowledge of some at least of these gentlemen would enable him to give the right hon. gentleman the information as to their character and standing. It is significant that in the handbook from which the hon. member from Jacques Cartier has quoted, the name of this firm does not appear at all among the shipping masters of Bordeaux.
I think I will be able to satisfy my hon. friend in a more direct manner by bringing down the correspondence we have on this subject.
From Mr. Fabre ?
From Mr. MacDonald, British consul at Bordeaux.
But Mr. Fabre is our own agent in France.
But France is a very large country, and Mr. MacDonald knows air. Colombier, and Mr. Fabre does not.

I presume Mr. Fabre is only a diplomatic agent.
Progress reported.
House again in Committee on Bill (No. 217) respecting penitentiaries.-The Minister of Justice.
On section 35,
Jlr. aiONK. Is this new ?
The ailNISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick). Only subsection (c) which is intended to facilitate improve-

ments without causing any unnecessary hardship.
Previous to this law in addition to the retiring allowance, there was, I think, a gratuity payable to the officers of the penitentiaries.

No. If they are paid a gratuity it is voted each year by the House.
On section 45,

This is for the purpose of protecting the penitentiaries against contagious and infectious diseases. Recently, when the small-pox was prevalent, we were obliged to receive prisoners into the penitentiary and to provide for them after we brought them there. Under this law, we will not he obliged to receive them until such time as they are certified to be well.
What will you do with them in the meantime ?

They remain under the control of the provincial authorities.
On section 50-juvenile offenders.found incorrigible, may be removed from reformatory to penitentiary.

If the offender is a small boy, I do not see anything in the clause to enable the warden to keep him separate from the old hardened criminals In the penitentiary. Should not some provision of that kind be made ? Otherwise his association with them might have a tendency to educate him in crime, and make him more disposed to commit crime when be came out than before.

Unfortunately, there is no such provision for the protection of the juvenile offender as the hon. gentleman suggests. Once a man gets into the penitentiary he is there with the other criminals, and there is no classification or separation with respect to the ages of the criminals. The juvenile offenders, as my hon. friend is aware, are detained in reformatory prisons ; but if it is there ascertained that a juvenile offender is quite beyond hope of being reformed lie may be removed from the penitentiary and dealt with there.
On section 56-if insane when term expires-discharged if not insane.

You make provision for two things here. You set apart a place for insane convicts in the penitentiary; but you provide as well that all convicts who are found upon examination by the surgeon to be insane may be sent to an asylum ; and you also provide that the warden of the asylum may send them to another penitentiary.

We have got an asylum for insane criminals at
Kingston to which we remove all such criminals in eastern Canada. With respect to British Columbia, we provide that an insane criminal in the penitentiary there shall be removed to the insane asylum of that province, as it would be out of the ques-ton to remove him to Kingston.
I think it would be important not to remove the insane criminals very far, but there might be a ward in every penitentiary set aside for such prisoners.

The modern practice is to consider these diseases as curable, and to deal with insane convicts in the same way as we would with other insane persons. In Kingston the hospital is really a section of the penitentiary.
Does the same surgeon attend them ?

At Kingston it is the same surgeon. He is a most competent man, and performs the duties most satisfactorily.
On section 66-misapplication of transportation money by discharged convicts.

This is new. Convicts who are supplied with conduct money in order to pay their way to the place whence they came, are In the habit of remaining about the town or place where the penitentiaries are situated, and become perfect nuisances. This provides that when a man is given money to leave the place, he should use it for that purpose.
But suppose he finds employment, would you compel him to leave the place ?

The point is well taken, and I shall let that section stand.	[DOT]
On Schedule A,
Is it the intention of the government to replace Dr. Ducliesneau, the present warden of St. Vincent do Paul ?
Yes.
Has he resigned ?
He sent in his resignation.
Who is replacing him ?
The deputy warden is acting in his stead, as is customary in such cases.
When is it intended to replace Dr. Duchesneau ?

Immediately after the session. I must really get some time to consider the condition of St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) will remember that we have had trouble there for many years. The

time lias come when we should deal with it so as to put tills penitentiary on the same level as the others, and endeavour to have about the same conditions prevail there as prevail in our penitentiaries generally.
Is the penitentiary in very bad condition at present ?

We have not had any special outbreak, but my hon. friend will remember that we had them there periodically. I would desire to see what can be done towards what I think the betterment of the penitentiary, to restore discipline and put the institution on a better footing than heretofore.
On schedule for Kingston penitentiary,
I see that the position of surgeon and medical superintendent of the insane ward are united. Is Dr. Phelan filling the two positions?
Yes.
Are the physicians who are employed in connection with the penitentiaries allowed to practice ?

No, and that has been made a grievance against the present government-that we have not allowed the physicians to practice outside. The law was amended in 1895, and the principle has been established ever since 1896, because new appointments since then have been made subject to the conditions that the appointees should give all their time to the institution, and not practice outside. That is the law. I may say, speaking generally and once for all with regard to this schedule of salaries, that the net result is to increase the salaries in the aggregate by about $7,200.

I see this schedule provides for the medical superintendent for the insane ward of Kingston penitentiary at $1,000. I understand that Kingston is the only penitentiary in which there is an insane ward, and that Dr. Phelan is able to attend to the insane ward as well as to the rest of the penitentiary. If you have a physician for the insane ward alone, it might amount to giving a man a sinecure at $1,000 a year.

So far as the insane ward is concerned we have an average of thirty patients there. Dr. Phelan now performs the services with respect to both that ward and the penitentiary generally; but it may happen that he may not continue. In that event, our intention was to have an ordinary surgeon appointed to attend to the wants of the penitentiary generally, to whom we would pay a salary of $1,600 a year, and it might be necessary to have a specialist for the insane ward to whom we would .pay .$1,000 a year. But. under this schedule, if both positions are held by one man. instead of paying $2,600, Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.
we take permission to pay $2,100. There is a reduction in the salary of the chief keeper from $1,200 to $900. Then we have a reduction in the salary of the hospital overseer and school instructor from $1,200 to $S00. The assistant hospital overseer and school instructor is reduced from $700 to $600.
Why are they reduced ?
Because the salaries paid heretofore are really more than they ought to have.
Perhaps the minister would tell us what salaries they previously got, and what salaries they are paid now ?

Take, for instance, the hospital overseer and instructor. Under the schedule he was entitled to $1,200, but as a matter of fact he has only been receiving $800. We have got a man perfectly competent to perform the duties of the office and who is content to perform them for $800. But under the schedule he is entitled to receive $1,200, and the life of the minister is made a burden to him until such time as that man gets all he possibly can get under the schedule. My hon. friend may have a similar experience himself if, by and by, he comes to administer this department ; if there is any leeway he will find that the officers will not give him any rest until they have reached the maximum. The chief keeper, for instance, at the present time receives $900, and has been paid that, though he is entitled to $1,200. I may say, speaking of the salaries generally, that are fixed in this schedule, they are the salaries that are actually paid, with one or two exceptions. There is no intention to interfere with the salary of any man that he is now actually receiving, there is no intention to reduce it But I want to eliminate the temptation of appointing men and giving them salaries in excess of what they are fairly entitled to ; especially do I want to relieve myself of the continual appeals that are being made to me to increase the salaries because the schedule provides for it.
I quite agree with what is being done. I do not think we should have a schedule of prices a great deal above what we can get the men for.

My attention has been drawn to a fact I overlooked. In speaking about changes, I forgot to mention there is an increase to the night keeper of $100. He Is now receiving $600, and because of the very arduous duties be performs we propose to increase his salary to $700.
I suppose he is a very good man ?
lie is. Speaking generally of the officials of the Kingston penitentiary, we have very little to complain of with respect to their qualifications and the services they render.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What is the denomination of the chaplains at the different penitentiaries ?

One Protestant and one Roman Catholic. At Kingston, St. Vincent de Paul and Dorchester, the Protestant chaplain is of the Church of England. The Protestant chaplain at Manitoba is a Methodist, and the one at British Columbia is a Presbyterian.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Are all the Protestant convicts at these penitentiaries members of the Church of England ?

That is a question I do not profess to have any special knowledge of. But I have a remedy to propose, that is, to allow each denomination in the locality where the penitentiary is situated, to send a clergyman to the penitentiary occasionally to minister to the convicts. When I proposed that amendment the last time the Bill was under consideration, it received a very cool reception, there was no desire to allow that to be done. Perhaps I ought to say this, that one of the agencies in this country to which we are most indebted for their services to the convicts is the Salvation Army. They have what they call the Prison Gate service by which they become acquainted with the prisoners that are about to be discharged, and keep in touch with them, meet them at the gates, and get employment for them. There is a large and important branch in Toronto who take charge of convicts discharged from the Kingston penitentiary, and I believe do them much good. 1 can say that that particular institution has done a very good service so far as my knowledge of their work in the penitentiaries go.

It seems to me the suggestion of the minister that a convict should be allowed the services of a minister belonging to the church to which he adhered, is a very good one. I cannot see why there can be any objection to it. I should think that almost any church might do for a convict when he goes to the penitentiary.

The minister spoke of the services rendered to convicts by the Salvation Army, and I think he spoke truly. I know something of what they have been doing in that line, and I think I would go a little further than the minister and, while recognizing the services of chaplains of other denominations, I would give a small amount to the Salvation Army to encourage them, for I believe they are doing better work than perhaps any other church along that line.
They are looking after the convicts after they come out, and that is very important, and they are trying to keep them from falling back into their old vices.

The Salvation Army have never suggested that they should receive any remuneration for any of the work they have done. The only request they ever made to me was that they should be allowed access to the convicts ; but it has never been suggested directly or indirectly that anything should be paid them for this work, in fact I do not think they have ever asked for remuneration.
On schedule for Manitoba Penitentiary,

The present schedule provides for a salary of $2,000 for the warden at the Manitoba penitentiary, but as a matter of fact he has been in receipt of a salary of $2,200 under the old schedule that existed previously to 1895. This provision authorizes the payment to him of the salary of which he is actually in receipt, $2,200. Everybody is aware that Colonel Irvine, the present warden, has been in the employ of the government a good many years and has done very good service indeed, and is a very competent officer.
On section 34,

I have just been reading over the suggestion which the hon. min-ter makes in regard to the chaplains, and it seems to me to be a very proper one. It is this :
The minister, instead of appointing a Protestant chaplain for any penitentiary, may direct that the clergymen of the different Protestant denominations represented in the community where a penitentiary is situate, shall be permitted to perform the duties of the Protestant chaplaincy in rotation, each in his turn taking a week, the assignment being under the direction of the warden, in which case the salary allowed for a Protestant chaplain shall be divided among the clergymen of the several denominations performing such duties in proportion to the time given to such duties by each.
I should certainly assent to that.
It seems very fair and proper. I beg to move to amend section 34 by adding that as subclause 2.
Do you intend to finish the Bill to-night 1

No.
Mr. WILSON Why not let that stand until to-morrow and take it up again ?
Very well.

I think it is worth thinking about.
Progress reported.
Mr. Speaker, as we have done a really very good day's work, and as an encouragement to our lion, friends on the other side of the House, I move that the House do now adjourn.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Lnurier).

speechtext: Before we adjourn I would like to ask my right lion, friend what business we will take up to-morrow ? Is it intended to go into Supply or to take up some other business ?
It is understood that we shall take up the Redistribution Bill.
Will we continue that Bill from day to day until we finish it ?
Oh, I was under the expectation that we would finish it in one day.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 9.50 p.m.
Wednesday, September 9, 1903.
